items.summary: Bubble-shaped Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) constitute a unique class of quantum fluids with a hollow, thin-shell geometry that supports a wide variety of phenomena that are distinct from those of compact condensates. Numerical simulation of such systems is particularly challenging due to their inherently three-dimensional structure and extreme aspect ratios. We present an efficient finite-difference simulation framework designed for solving partial differential equations in such nontrivial topologies with a focus on the static and dynamical modeling of bubble-shaped BECs. By employing selective spatial sampling on a semi-structured grid, our method substantially reduces memory usage and achieves more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in computational performance compared to conventional split-step Fourier solvers. The algorithm is naturally extendable for highly parallel execution on GPUs, enabling large-scale, time-dependent simulations of thin-shell condensates. We apply this framework to simulate the formation of bubble BECs through a controlled hollowing-out protocol using ab initio trapping potentials relevant to the Cold Atom Laboratory aboard the International Space Station. From these simulations, we identify characteristic timescales and parameter ramps required to achieve adiabatic evolution, thereby assessing the feasibility of experimentally realizing bubble-shaped condensates in microgravity environments.

items.title: Collective-Variable Stein Variational Gradient Descent for Free Energy Surface Exploration
items.summary: Enhanced-sampling methods enable molecular simulations to access configurational regions that are difficult to explore with conventional dynamics, but their efficiency often deteriorates as the number of collective variables (CVs) increases. Here, we introduce an enhanced-sampling framework that couples Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) with parallel restrained molecular dynamics simulations to facilitate exploration of higher-dimensional CV spaces. SVGD collectively transports an ensemble of interacting particles toward a target probability distribution by combining mean forces that guide particles toward low-free-energy regions with kernel-mediated repulsive interactions that maintain particle diversity. We validate the approach using an analytically solvable double-well model, followed by aqueous alanine dipeptide and tripeptide in two- and four-dimensional CV spaces, respectively. In each case, the particle ensemble reproduces the corresponding target distribution, and the reconstructed free-energy surfaces agree closely with analytical or umbrella-sampling references. For alanine dipeptide and tripeptide, CV-SVGD requires substantially less aggregate MD sampling than the corresponding umbrella-sampling reference calculations. These results demonstrate the potential of CV-SVGD as a flexible, parallelizable framework for enhanced sampling in multidimensional CV spaces. We additionally provide an open-source Python implementation to facilitate its adoption.

items.title: Field demonstration of a self-contained 10 km mobile-to-ground quantum network node via common-aperture co-propagation
items.summary: In this work, we demonstrate a dual-function, common-aperture free-space optical system that simultaneously supports decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) at 803 nm and bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link from a mobile platform to a stationary ground station. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture architecture where a co-propagating classical optical link simultaneously performs full QKD post-processing and ecrypted payload transmission over a 10 km atmospheric channel. The classical link utilizes Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of $\sim$ 0.4 $\%$ (estimated bit error rate (BER) of 3.13 $\times$ 10$^{-5}$) with hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission. Over the 10.31 km link, the QKD system achieved an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 2.512 $\%$ and an average secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Finally, using the distilled keys, real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission was executed over the co-aligned classical optical channel, proving the feasibility of a completely self-contained, jam resistant mobile quantum optical network.

items.title: Percolation Transition of K-Destinations Reveals Universal Backbone of Urban Mobility Networks
items.summary: Cities are held together by a small subset of recurrent origin--destination ties, but extracting this backbone from noisy mobility data remains difficult, and most models still prioritize distance over connectivity. We build directed mobility networks from 48 months of mobile-phone data across eight U.S. cities (2018--2021) and apply a rank-based percolation filter that retains, for each origin, its top-K destinations. Defining K* as the smallest cutoff that yields a strongly connected network, we find that city-specific thresholds cluster tightly across space and time, with a representative value near $K\approx130$. Degree-preserving and gravity-style baselines do not recover this scale, underscoring the importance of selectively preserved long-range functional ties. We then define PPD(K), an origin-level mobility concentration measure, and show that socioeconomic associations peak around the percolation-derived integration regime. Together, these findings offer a principled method to extract a minimal mobility backbone and connect its structure to persistent socioeconomic variation.

items.title: P-ONE-1: the first detector line of the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment
items.summary: Neutrino telescopes instrument optically transparent media with three-dimensional arrays of photosensors to detect Cherenkov radiation induced by neutrino interactions within or near the instrumented volume. The small cross-sections of the weak interaction and the low neutrino fluxes above TeV energies require vast detector volumes, which only natural media on Earth can realistically provide. Spurred by the detection of the first neutrino sources by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a new generation of neutrino telescopes is emerging to increase the global instrumented volume and detection sensitivity. The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) aims to install such a telescope in the Northeast Pacific Ocean, building on established neutrino telescope design targets in collaboration with Ocean Networks Canada (ONC). This article presents the design, integration, and testing of the first P-ONE line, P-ONE-1, in preparation for its deployment and integration into ONC's deep-sea observatory NEPTUNE. Alongside the detector design and integration methods, we detail in-air and in-water system-level validation performed at several test sites in Canada, culminating in the successful construction of P-ONE-1 and its preparation for deployment.

items.title: Fully Automated Wannier Disentanglement via Projectability Selection in Gaussian and Augmented Plane-Wave Frameworks
items.summary: Constructing the frozen manifold for entangled bands requires balancing exact reproduction of the target bands with sufficient variational freedom to build a well-localized subspace from the broader Bloch pool. We present a workflow that systematically determines the energy ceiling for a target number of selected Wannier projections, freezing every Bloch state below this threshold across the sampled k-mesh. By measuring projectability, the spectral weight of each Bloch state projected onto the target localized basis, the workflow detects missing conduction channels and quantifies discrepancies between orbital character and energy-based freezing. In comparisons where we controlled the extent of the energy ceiling, freezing all sub-ceiling states is generally favored over projectability-based frozen states. Of the seven materials we tested, freezing all sub-ceiling states lowers the band error on four from between 11 meV and 1.2 eV to 18 meV or less, and matches the projectability-based choice to within about 2 meV on the remaining three. In each of the four, projectability-based frozen states give the lower spread, showing that spread alone cannot identify the better model. With the frozen states held fixed, the workflow minimizes the gauge-invariant spread, constructs the gauge from density-matrix columns on atomic orbitals, and passes an isolated set of bands to Wannier90 for localization. The workflow is implemented in two programs for seamless high-throughput Wannierization with WIEN2k (wien2wannier) and CRYSTAL (LCAO2Wannier). Using a single set of calibrated defaults, the CRYSTAL implementation with analytic overlaps produces models that reproduce the reference bands of five cells, from bulk h-BN in a joint valence-and-conduction model to a magnetic framework with 1424 orbitals. The WIEN2k implementation produces eight such models from seven calculations.

items.title: Basin-Specific Changes and Intensity of Tropical Cyclones
items.summary: The 1990-2024 North Atlantic trend in the proportion of major-cyclone Category 3-5 fixes among all Category 1-5 fixes (the Kossin ratio, KR) was about five times the combined Pacific trend. This contrast motivates examining their basin-specific links: aerosol loading to cyclone potential intensity, and potential intensity to observed cyclone activity. Annual increases in aerosol loading were generally associated with decreasing potential intensity both in the North Atlantic and in all three Pacific basins. Potential intensity changes were consistently positively associated with cyclone-fix count changes in the North Atlantic, in some specifications also in the eastern North Pacific and South Pacific. However, changes in potential intensity in the western North Pacific were significantly negatively correlated with fix-count changes. The negative association disappeared after controlling for El Niño-Southern Oscillation changes. Furthermore, annual potential intensity changes were never significantly positively associated with KR changes.

items.title: Multifractality of human upper-limb velocity tracks motor optimization via hand dominance experiment
items.summary: Theoretical goal-directed movements follow a unique, stereotyped velocity profile, but continuous movement has no unique optimal solution, so it is unclear whether motor optimization makes continuous movement more stereotyped or more diverse. Previous studies indicated higher information content in the dominant hand, suggesting greater diversity. Because continuous velocity is a composition of overlapping joints movement of varying form, timing and amplitude, comparable to the events that compose spike trains and heartbeat series, we asked whether this diversity appears as a wider multifractal spectrum of velocity. We applied multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis to motion-capture velocity of cursive handwriting from right- and left-handed participants writing with both hands; hand dominance is a natural experiment in which task and geometry are fixed while optimization varies. With the dominant hand, spectra were wider, had a lower dominant exponent and were more positively asymmetric in both groups, whereas hands with the same functional role did not differ between groups. A logistic regression on the three spectral features identified the dominant hand with a cross-validated AUC of up to 0.93. Optimized continuous movement is thus not more stereotyped but more diverse: complex, neither stereotyped nor random, with multifractality that tracks hand dominance.

items.title: Generation of non-Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions during thermalization of interacting baths
items.summary: We report on numerical experiments of thermalization between two reservoirs in which interspecies interactions are mediated via a Hamiltonian with a Gaussian dependence upon the distance between the particles. By using relatively high statistics, we are able to study deviations from the initially imprinted Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions as a function of the range and strength of the interaction, as well as the parameters of the two baths such as masses, trapping frequencies, that strongly affect the spatial overlap of the two species. At large interaction strengths and for any range, deviations are attributable to the sudden conversion of latent interaction energy into kinetic energy of the particles. In addition, long range interactions generate deviations even for interaction strengths in the weak regime, and non-uniform confinement introduces a further source of deviation from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution. This latter results in transient two temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions suggestive of an inverse cascading route from inter-particle dynamics to thermalization. In the weakly-interacting regime, a simple expression for the equilibrium temperature is also obtained and discussed. These findings may be of relevance in the dynamics of exothermic chemical reactions, in the physics of ultracold atomic mixtures, and in self-sustained burning plasmas.

items.title: Physical Processes Driving Year-to-Year Surface Temperature Variability Changes in a Warming Climate
items.summary: Under anthropogenic greenhouse forcing, climate models project a decrease in year-to-year temperature variability in the mid-to-high latitudes and an increase in the tropics and subtropics. Here, we examine year-to-year temperature variability in the CESM Large Ensemble in concert with an idealized stochastic moist energy balance model (SMEBM) with effective surface heat capacity and local feedback parameter specified based on CESM. We find that the zonal-mean CESM variability change pattern largely persists after filtering out the impact of El Niño. The SMEBM largely captures this change pattern. In the SMEBM, changes in the mid-to-high latitudes are driven by changes in the effective heat capacity due to sea ice retreat, combined with changes in anomalous moist static energy convergence modulated by the polar-amplified time-mean temperature change. The CESM local feedback parameter evolves to be less stabilizing in the low latitudes, which causes tropical and subtropical variability to increase in the SMEBM.

items.title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
items.summary: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $κ$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.

items.title: Why Hadamard states?
items.summary: In QFT on curved spacetime, the Hadamard condition is often presented as a necessary condition on 'physically reasonable' states of the quantum field, and plays a central role in many theoretical and foundational applications - ranging from proofs of the renormalizability of Wick polynomials to derivations of the Hawking temperature. Yet despite this, the philosophical and foundational underpinnings of the Hadamard condition remain murky. I critically discuss existing motivations for the Hadamard condition in the literature, before arguing in favour of an alternative motivation for the Hadamard condition, according to which it is best understood as a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a well-defined operator product of a certain form on a sufficiently large space of observables of the quantum field, satisfying a variety of further conditions. This clarifies the role and status of the Hadamard condition, including its relationship to the equivalence principle, to well-definedness of physical quantities such as Wick polynomials and the expectation value of the stress-energy operator, and the sense in which Hadamard states are 'vacuum-like'.

items.title: Reaction-induced Localized Annealing for On-chip Materials Discovery
items.summary: On-chip thermal processing is a key technology for materials discovery across all disciplines of the natural sciences. Here, we present a microfabricated heat-delivery platform that enables reaction-induced localized on-chip annealing up to 1400°C. A buried reactive multilayer combined with a nanometric diffusion barrier provide ultra-fast heating and quenching rates on the order of 10$^6$°C s$^{-1}$ as illustrated by the generation of ultra-high aspect ratio microstructures during rapid-solidification and the stabilization of dopant-free tetragonal zirconia at room temperature. Rapid kinetics also enable the observation of transient states of capillary-driven hole collapse in melts. Our work expands localized high-temperature processing routes and offers a material-independent approach for rapid screening of multidimensional nanomaterials on and off-equilibrium.

items.title: Performance of the TUCAN Magnetically Shielded Room
items.summary: The TRIUMF Ultracold Advanced Neutron (TUCAN) collaboration has commissioned a large magnetically shielded room to be used for measuring the neutron electric dipole moment (nEDM) to a precision of $10^{-27}~e\mathrm{cm}$. The room is composed of five layers of MuMetal and one layer of copper and sits within the $\lesssim 370~μ\mathrm{T}$ ambient field produced by the TRIUMF cyclotron. Within this environment, the quasi-static shielding factor was measured to be $2.95(2) \times 10^4$ at $0.01~\mathrm{Hz}$ with an external peak-to-peak perturbation of $2~μ\mathrm{T}$. Without the large ambient cyclotron field, the shielding factor improves to $3.40(3)\times 10^4$ at the same perturbation amplitude and frequency. After idealization in the cyclotron field, the residual field at the room center was $B = 1.8(2)~\mathrm{nT}$ and the vertical first-order gradient across the central 1~m$^3$ ($dB_{\mathrm{z}}/dz$) was $-307(26)~\mathrm{pT/m}$. With additional improvement to the idealization, and with active compensation, we expect the room to be adequate for a $10^{-27}~e\mathrm{cm}$ nEDM search.

items.title: Determination of the Human-Robot Interaction Workspace for Robot Assisted Head Stabilization Control
items.summary: Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.

items.title: Formation of a Vorticity Singularity in an Axisymmetric Poloidal Flow
items.summary: In this work, building on previous studies of plane-parallel flows, we investigate the rapid growth of the frozen-in vorticity field in an axisymmetric poloidal flow. We present the results of numerical simulations performed using supercomputing resources. We show that exponentially growing velocity gradients can develop on the axis of symmetry, while vorticity gradients grow superexponentially. These results are qualitatively similar to those previously obtained for vorticity in a simpler two-dimensional flow.

items.title: Machine-learned spectral PDE solvers for fluids and plasmas
items.summary: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.

items.title: Theoretical Description of Electronic Modulation and Superconducting Coherence
items.summary: An electronic modulation can retain a substantial local amplitude while its translational coherence is limited by spatial disorder. Its coupling to superconductivity therefore cannot be characterized by a single modulation intensity. We develop a phenomenological formulation of a finite-wave-vector complex electronic envelope coupled to a charged superconducting field. Translation and gauge symmetries constrain the interaction terms, while amplitude, modulation-gradient and condensate-gradient couplings act on distinct responses. The resulting variational equations give uniform coexistence conditions, local stability criteria and phase-gradient coefficients. We define the helicity modulus by a boundary twist, distinguish phase-only from amplitude-weighted correlations, and give an explicit minimal spectral Hamiltonian illustrating how the electronic texture may enter momentum-resolved measurements. The proposed tests use distinct spatial, spectral and stiffness observables; none assumes that a tunnelling gap directly measures condensate amplitude. An explicit kernel expansion yields the leading displacement of the selected wave vector, while the thermodynamic twist response determines phase rigidity independently of charge intensity. The analytical relations and selected numerical responses distinguish amplitude, spatial organization and condensate rigidity within the specified coupled-field model.

items.title: Conservation of Momentum and Energy in the Lorenz-Abraham-Dirac Equation of Motion
items.summary: After a brief review of the modified (by transition forces) causal Lorentz-Abraham (LA) classical equation of motion for an extended charged sphere and its limit to the mass-renormalized modified causal Lorentz-Abraham-Dirac (LAD) equation of motion as the radius of the charged sphere approaches zero, a concise derivation is given for the conditions on the velocity and external force required for these modified equations of motion to satisfy conservation of momentum and energy. The effects of mass renomalization on the radiated momentum-energy is clarified. The solutions to the unmodified LAD equation of motion, the causal modified LA and LAD equations of motion, and the Landau-Lifshitz approximate solution to the unmodified LAD equation of motion are obtained for a charge traveling through a parallel-plate capacitor.

items.title: District Size Matters: How Seats Per District Shapes Proportionality Under STV
items.summary: We study the impact of utilizing multimember districts and Single Transferable Vote (STV) as the winner selection method on partisan proportionality. We start with detailed case studies of the upper legislative houses of Illinois, New Hampshire, and New Mexico, building ensembles of redistricting maps with mostly 2-member, mostly 3-member, and mostly 4-member districts for each state. These ensembles are constructed using two methods: building from precincts, and merging currently existing single-member districts. We also compare two ballot generation models for each experiment: a modified Bradley-Terry model and a Plackett-Luce model. We find that our ensembles of multimember districts paired with STV have results which are centered closer to partisan proportionality than when single member districts are used. However, the choice of district size affects partisan outcomes enough that this choice could be exploited by a partisan mapmaker to advantage a particular party. The findings are consistent across all combinations of district construction and ballot generation models within a single state. We then expand our study to 41 different states, obtaining consistently similar proportionality results and allowing us to empirically evaluate the two ballot generation models, as implemented in VoteKit, at a national scale.

items.title: Counterexamples to the total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture
items.summary: The total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture asserts that the ground-state particle density and total current determine the scalar potential up to an additive constant and the vector potential up to a gauge transformation. We give three counterexamples for two spinless fermions in the physically relevant setting of three spatial dimensions. In each, a Hamiltonian $H^{v,\mathbf{A}}$ has a nondegenerate ground state with identically zero total current but nonzero magnetic field. Complex conjugation then yields a second Hamiltonian $H^{v,-\mathbf{A}}$, with the same scalar potential and interaction, whose ground state has the same density and the same zero current, while the magnetic field is reversed. The first two examples are noninteracting. One is explicit, with a smooth bounded vector potential and a Gaussian density. The other has smooth bounded scalar and vector potentials in the standard potential spaces. The third example has Coulomb repulsion with unit coupling, an isotropic harmonic scalar potential, and Dirac monopole fields of magnetic charge $\pm 1/2$. The monopole example uses vector potentials defined on separate spatial patches, since these fields are not curls of globally defined smooth vector potentials.

items.title: Time-resolved Rydberg dynamics in molecules
items.summary: We develop a general theoretical framework for the ultrafast dynamics of coherently populated autoionizing Rydberg states in molecules, whose coherent decay results in asymmetric Fano line shapes produced by interference between resonant autoionization and direct ionization. The asymmetric line shapes form in the photoelectron continuum during the autoionization lifetime of the decreasing Rydberg population. By parameterizing autoionization resonances and solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, we model the buildup of the Fano profile together with the decline of the coherently excited Rydberg-state population. We compare our calculated photoelectron yields with the XUV-pump--IR-probe photoemission experiment of Biswas et al., Phys. Rev. A 110, 043106 (2024), in which neutral ground-state CO$_2$ molecules are excited by an XUV pulse to the Henning sharp and diffuse Rydberg series and subsequently ionized by the delayed IR pulse. Based on our numerically modeled photoelectron yields, we analyze two complementary processes: (i) photoemission into the $X^2Π_g$ continuum of residual CO$_2^+$ ions, which exposes interferences between direct photoionization and excited-state autoionization, and (ii) IR-induced photoemission into the CO$_2^+$[$B^2Σ_u^+$] continuum, which reveals quantum beats between Rydberg states. Our close-coupling model provides a versatile, extendable framework for tracking molecular Rydberg-state relaxation and, more generally, light-driven coherent dynamics in complex quantum systems.

items.title: NeRF-Inspired Neural Fields for 3D Super-resolution of Reacting-Flows
items.summary: The multiscale nature of turbulent reacting flows and the importance of fine-scale structures pose challenges for super-resolution. We investigate a 3D super-resolution framework inspired by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), called Neural Field Super-Resolution (NFSR), to reconstruct fine-resolution fields from coarsened reacting-flow fields. The proposed formulation adapts the continuous coordinate-conditioned representation of NeRF to physical flow-field reconstruction by conditioning spatial coordinates with local coarse-grid thermochemical information, while eliminating radiance prediction and volume rendering. Principal component analysis is used to provide a compact and low-dimensional representation of the thermochemical state, and a hierarchical extension, H-NFSR, progressively reconstructs the solution through intermediate resolution levels. The framework is evaluated using three-dimensional direct numerical simulation data for a turbulent premixed hydrogen-air flame, with an overall spatial coarsening factor of eight in each coordinate direction. The results demonstrate consistently better prediction measures and a higher ability to reconstruct fine-scale information than tricubic interpolation on the unseen test realization. The hierarchical formulation reduces visible coarse-cell imprinting. In contrast, biased sampling mainly benefits the most localized structures. Three-dimensional isosurface comparisons further show that H-NFSR recovers much of the small and intermediate features of the flow, including surface wrinkling and local flame curvature effects. These results highlight the potential of coordinate-conditioned neural fields as a flexible framework for three-dimensional coarse-to-fine reconstruction of reacting-flow simulations.

items.title: Time-Reversal and Reversible Dynamics in Cavity QED for Quantum Metrology
items.summary: Quantum-enhanced metrology relies on entanglement to achieve sensitivities beyond the standard quantum limit. While remarkable progress has been made in generating highly entangled many-body states, extracting their metrological advantage remains a central challenge because the encoded information is often inaccessible to realistic measurements. A key development of the past decade has been the realization that many-body interactions can play a dual role: they can be used not only to generate entanglement, but also to decode it. This idea underlies interaction-based readout and time-reversal protocols, in which controlled non-linear dynamics transform weakly encoded signals into experimentally accessible observables. Cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) provides a particularly powerful setting for these approaches because it combines collective enhancement, tunable interactions, and controllable reversibility within a single platform. In this review, we discuss the emergence of time-reversal protocols in cavity QED, from their conceptual roots in Loschmidt echoes to modern implementations of signal amplification through a time-reversed interaction (SATIN), scrambling-enhanced metrology, and more general interaction-based readout schemes. We examine the physical mechanisms that enable reversible many-body dynamics, review key experimental demonstrations, and discuss future directions involving complex entangled states, nonlinear decoding, and emerging quantum platforms. Together, these developments suggest that the ability to decode quantum information may become as important as the ability to generate it, establishing reversible many-body dynamics as a central resource for quantum-enhanced sensing.

items.title: The optical force on a dielectric slab
items.summary: Radiation-pressure forces on transmissive optics, including dynamical backaction, are usually computed from the momentum flux of the external fields. For a dielectric of finite thickness, this omits the time dependence of the electromagnetic momentum stored inside. We compute the force on a lossless dielectric slab of arbitrary thickness $L_s$ submerged in a dielectric fluid, proceeding from both Lorentz force on its bound charges and from the external momentum fluxes for arbitrary carrier and sideband fields. We treat the surrounding medium through a prescribed linear dielectric response and do not model the accompanying mechanical response of the fluid, including pressure and electrostriction. These two methods both recover the expected force in the limit of a thin reflector, but differ in the more general case by the rate of change of the field momentum stored in the slab. This storage term vanishes for static fields and at low frequencies reduces to $(L_s/c^2)\,dP/dt$, where $P$ is the net power through the slab. In a cavity, where $P$ depends on the slab position, the storage term produces a velocity-dependent force. The Abraham and Minkowski momentum formulations applied to the storage term are reconciled to give an unambiguous force on the dielectric in the case of an exterior vacuum environment, where there is no fluid response to model.

items.title: Inference of Hierarchical Core-Periphery Structure in Temporal Networks
items.summary: Networks can have various types of mesoscale structures. One such structure is core--periphery structure, which consists of sets of densely-connected core nodes and sets of sparsely-connected peripheral nodes. Core nodes are connected densely to other core nodes and are potentially connected densely to peripheral nodes, which are connected sparsely to other nodes. There has been much research on core--periphery structure in time-independent networks, but few core--periphery detection methods have been developed for time-dependent (i.e., ``temporal") networks. Using a multilayer-network representation of temporal networks and an inference approach that employs stochastic block models, we generalize a recent method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure \cite{Polanco23} from time-independent networks to temporal networks. In contrast to ``onion-like'' nested core--periphery structures (where each node is assigned to a group according to how deeply it is nested in a network's core), hierarchical core--periphery structures encompass networks with nested structures, tree-like structures (where any two groups must either be disjoint or have one group as a strict subset of the other group), and general non-nested mesoscale structures (where the group assignments of nodes do not have to be nested in any way). To perform statistical inference and thereby identify hierarchical core--periphery structure, we use a Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. We illustrate our method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure in one synthetic temporal network and two real-world temporal networks, and we discuss the structures that we identify in these networks.

items.title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations
items.summary: We present a perturbation-based theoretical framework, together with its immersed boundary/volume penalization implementation, for long-time simulations of fully resolved rigid-particle dynamics in acoustically actuated flows. A perturbation formulation separates the fast acoustic time scale from the slow mean dynamics, avoiding long-time direct integration of the fully compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The immersed rigid body is represented through a Brinkman penalization term in equations posed over a unified fluid-solid domain. The coupled fluid-particle system is decomposed into a time-harmonic first-order problem governing the acoustic response and a time-averaged second-order problem. A central challenge in this decomposition is the treatment of the moving fluid-solid interface. We derive order-consistent expressions for the structural velocities, comprising rigid-body and Stokes-drift contributions, and formulate the corresponding first- and second-order rigid-body equations of motion. For a circular particle in two dimensions, the simulations reveal substantial differences in the magnitude and structure of acoustic streaming around fixed and freely moving particles, highlighting the importance of two-way fluid-structure coupling. The results also show that particle-density effects are more complex than suggested by simplified descriptions based solely on the acoustic contrast factor. The framework captures the mean particle dynamics using time steps associated with the slow particle-motion scale rather than the much smaller acoustic time scale. Finally, simulations of an elliptical particle demonstrate the ability of the method to capture coupled translational and rotational motion. The proposed approach therefore provides an efficient route to fully resolved, long-time simulations of acoustically driven rigid-particle motion while retaining two-way fluid-structure coupling.

items.title: Controlling Optical Quantum Interference with Plasmonic Metasurfaces
items.summary: The ability to efficiently control optical quantum interference by the same device is a challenging task that promises to enable key operations in quantum information processing. Here, we tackle this problem by presenting a composite quantum plasmonic metasurface operating as an ultrathin non-unitary beamsplitter capable of achieving both single photon bosonic bunching and fermionic anti-bunching interference just by varying the incident photons frequency or changing the design dimensions. The presented metasurface combines a plasmonic grating corrugated by periodic nanoslits that can achieve extraordinary optical transmission with additional nanostripes on top forming nanocavities characterized by localized gap plasmon resonances. The photon-photon interactions are analyzed based on calculating the quantum coalescence metric which accurately portrays the obtained bunching or anti-bunching quantum interference. The presented quantum interference operation is applicable to both fundamental non-classical light interactions and in the design of more applied quantum optical logic gates used in quantum computing and communications.

items.title: A Neural Implicit Flow Super-Resolution Approach for Reacting Flows
items.summary: We present a novel framework for reconstructing fine-resolution scalar fields from coarse-resolution data in 2D unsteady flames using an extension of neural implicit flow (NIF). The framework leverages the novel architecture of NIF to develop an efficient representation of scalar fields in spatio-temporal reacting flows. Different strategies are adopted within the proposed framework to establish super-resolution for multiscalar fields in combustion. They include 1) a reconfiguration of the input and output fields, 2) the use of a latent composition space based on nonlinear principal component analysis (NLPCA) to reconstruct the fine-resolution fields, and the conversion from nonlinear principal components (NLPCs) to species and temperature contours, and 3) the adoption of multiple ParameterNets in the NIF architecture, each accommodating one of the NLPCs. The framework was validated on a 2D unsteady Bunsen-stabilized lean premixed methane-air flame with forcing at the inlet. The results, using a coarsening ratio of 8 in a given direction, show that the adoption of multiple ParameterNets yields more accurate super-resolution than a single ParameterNet without any additional cost in the hyperparameters.

items.title: DeGroot Dynamics on Multiplex Networks with Directed and Acyclic Interlayer Connectivities
items.summary: In models of opinion dynamics, researchers typically examine how an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced by the opinions of their neighbors in a network. However, people's opinions on a topic are also influenced by their opinions and their neighbors' opinions on related topics. In an election, for example, the opinions of a voter on a variety of issues inform their opinions of electoral candidates. To consider the influence between people's opinions on multiple distinct topics, we study a multiplex extension of the traditional DeGroot consensus model. In our multiplex DeGroot model, different network layers represent distinct topics and directed interlayer edges (which are not allowed to form cycles) encode relationships between distinct topics. In our model, an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced both by the opinions of their neighbors on that topic and by their own opinions on related topics. We prove under mild conditions that our multiplex DeGroot model converges to a limit state. We also prove that strong connectedness in ``source layers'' (which represent fundamental beliefs) eventually yields a consensus opinion in each layer. In particular, we show that consensus on source layers can lead to consensus on other layers even when those layers otherwise would be polarized. By numerically simulating our multiplex DeGroot model on a two-layer network, we examine the effects on opinion dynamics of (1) different network structures and (2) different types of initial opinion data.

items.title: Analytical Chemistry at the Planetary Frontier
items.summary: Planetary science depends on chemical measurements made under conditions very different from those in a terrestrial laboratory. This review treats the analytical methods of planetary science as one connected chain, from orbital remote sensing through in-situ measurements by landers and rovers and sample collection and curation, to the micro-analysis of returned material on Earth. Orbital methods, including visible and near-infrared reflectance, thermal emission and gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy, are discussed first. In-situ techniques are then reviewed, including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), micro-focus X-ray fluorescence (XRF), deep-ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence spectroscopy, evolved gas analysis with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and miniaturized mass spectrometry. Contamination control and curation practices are described, followed by laboratory techniques such as secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS and NanoSIMS), atom probe tomography (APT), thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS), synchrotron micro-XRF and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy. Accuracy, calibration and reference materials are discussed as the link between in-situ and laboratory data, and the role of chemometrics and data fusion is examined. Flight and laboratory instruments are compared in terms of spatial resolution, detection limit, sample consumption and throughput. Active neutron-gamma spectroscopy planned for the Dragonfly mission to Titan is also discussed. This comparison shows that in-situ and laboratory techniques are complementary. In-situ instruments provide context and select samples, while laboratory techniques provide isotopic, molecular and speciation data that cannot yet be obtained in situ.

items.title: Decoding Transient X-ray Absorption Spectra of Acetylacetone With Multireference Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Theory
items.summary: Time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) offers an element- and site-specific probe of coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics, but its interpretation requires methods that can treat multiconfigurational excited states across nonequilibrium nuclear ensembles. Here, we report time-resolved simulations of the acetylacetone (AcAc) transient X-ray absorption spectra by combining surface-hopping dynamics from complete active space second-order perturbation theory with multireference algebraic diagrammatic construction (MR-ADC). The simulated 20-200 fs spectra show a good agreement with experimental measurements and reveal that the TR-XAS response is governed by continuously evolving distributions of molecular geometries on the singlet potential energy surfaces (S2 and S1). In particular, absorption at 279.5-281.5 eV is enhanced for transient, nearly symmetric proton-sharing configurations, whereas the 284-286 eV profile reflects geometry-dependent C1s excitations modulated by proton transfer, bond alternation, and ring opening. For the long-time T_1 spectrum (7-10 ps), the principal features near 281.4 and 283.8 eV are assigned to central C 1s excitations into low-lying triplet pi-orbitals. Together, our simulations provide a more complete mechanistic picture of AcAc photorelaxation by directly linking ultrafast carbon K-edge signals to proton transfer, skeletal reorganization, internal conversion, and triplet formation.

items.title: Allight: A Perfect Photon Collector
items.summary: Collecting photons from quantum emitters remains a key limitation in light-matter interaction because conventional lenses collect light only from one direction. Here, we introduce a perfect light collector by inverse-designing a surrounding dielectric structure that encloses the emitter to increase photon-collection efficiency toward unity. Decomposing the device into several refractive interfaces enables emission collection from the full 4$π$ solid angle with adiabatic reshaping into a collimated beam. We experimentally demonstrate, in two dimensions, the ray bending that collimates omnidirectional emission. Our collector transforms current paradigms for highly efficient photon collection from narrowband, cavity-based techniques into experimentally robust, broadband, non-resonant dielectric devices.

items.title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
items.summary: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

items.title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
items.summary: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.

items.title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
items.summary: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

items.title: Testing the statistical compatibility of data sets with a common prior
items.summary: The Parameter Goodness-of-fit (PG) test [hep-ph/0304176] offers a simple test statistic to study the compatibility of different data sets within a given theoretical model. In its original formulation it assumes that the data sets are statistically independent. We propose an extension of the PG test for the situation when some parameters of the model are constrained by an auxiliary data set called prior here. As the prior is imposed for all data sets, they are no longer statistically independent. We show that under the Gaussian approximation, the prior-constrained PG test statistic follows a generalised $χ^2$ distribution, which can be used to obtain $p$-values in a straight-forward way. In the approximation of a strong prior constraint, the test converges towards the standard PG test for the unconstrained model parameters.

items.title: Scaling H2 Factorization to Billion-Unknown Three-Dimensional Problems
items.summary: Strong recursive skeletonization provides approximate direct solvers for dense matrices from integral equations and kernel methods, but distributed implementations face substantial communication costs and limited parallelism, especially in three dimensions. We present a distributed-memory $\mathcal{H}^2$ factorization solver for symmetric matrices that combines spatial box coloring, delayed Schur complement updates, streamed sketching-based interpolative decomposition, and BLAS-3 and shared-memory kernels. Spatial coloring enables every process to participate in each boundary stage, while delayed updates and streamed sketching reduce dense storage and communication. To our knowledge, this is the first distributed-memory strong recursive skeletonization factorization demonstrated for three-dimensional volume integral equations at billion-unknown scale. Experiments on up to 512 compute nodes demonstrate factorization of a three-dimensional Laplace system with 3.62 billion unknowns, alongside three-dimensional Helmholtz tests and a two-dimensional Matérn system with 268 million unknowns. Combining streamed sketching and fully delayed updates reduces factorization time by $6.9\times$ for Laplace and $8.5\times$ for Helmholtz relative to the unsketched, eager configuration, while reducing maximum per-process resident memory by 57\% and 54\%, respectively.

items.title: Generalized Kahler BHE threefolds
items.summary: We study the notion of generalized Kahler Bismut--Hermitian--Einstein (GKBHE) manifolds, namely generalized Kähler manifolds for which both Bismut Ricci forms vanish, and we develop a theory for such structures on compact threefolds. We organize the analysis according to the horizontal rank, an invariant taking values in $\{0,1,2\}$ that measures the relative position of the canonical foliations associated with the two Hermitian structures. We characterize the case of horizontal rank $0$ (which corresponds to Kähler Ricci flat geometry) and describe the case of horizontal rank $1$, revealing its close interplay with the steady $ν$-soliton equation in Kähler geometry. This description also provides a tool for constructing new compact GKBHE threefolds.

items.title: Temporal Exploration and Rendezvous via Weisfeiler-Leman Colorings
items.summary: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edge relation changes in discrete time steps. The Temporal Exploration Problem (TEXP) asks for a temporal walk that visits all vertices. We show that every connected temporal graph with $n$ vertices can be explored in $O(qn\log^3(n))$ time steps, where $q$ is the number of vertex color classes induced by the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (2-WL) coloring. For small $q$, our bound substantially improves on the known worst-case bound of $Θ(n^2)$ in general connected temporal graphs. A corresponding walk can be constructed in deterministic polynomial time. The upper bound is complemented by lower bounds of $Ω(n\log(n))$ when $q$ is constant and $Ω(qn)$ when $1 \leq q \leq n$. We also apply our techniques to the Temporal Rendezvous Problem (TRP), in which two agents that do not communicate have to meet on a vertex of the temporal graph. Our exploration algorithm yields that, with only polynomial-time computational power, the agents can meet in $O(n\log^3(n))$ time steps, leaving a gap of only $\log^2(n)$ to the known lower bound. Dogeas, Erlebach, Kammer, Meintrup, and Moses Jr. [ICALP'24] have shown an $O(rn^{1+ε})$ bound for TEXP, for every fixed $ε> 0$, where $r$ is the number of orbits, and an $O(n^{1+ε})$ bound for TRP. Both results require superpolynomial computation time. Our contribution improves upon these results in several ways. First, the dependence on $n$ in the upper bounds on the number of time steps is decreased from $n^{1+ε}$ to $n\log^3(n)$ for both TEXP and TRP. Second, for TEXP, we bound the number of time steps linearly by the parameter q, which is efficiently computable and upper bounded by $r$. Third, we provide novel deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for both TEXP and TRP.

items.title: Level 2.5 large deviations and uncertainty relations for non-Markov self-interacting dynamics
items.summary: We address the general problem of formulating the dynamical large deviations of non-Markovian systems in a closed form. Specifically, we consider a broad class of ``self-interacting'' jump processes whose dynamics depends on the past through a functional of a state-dependent empirical observable. Exploiting a natural separation of timescales, \newnewtext{and under the corresponding mixing conditions,} we obtain the exact (so-called ``level 2.5'') large deviation joint statistics of the empirical measure over configurations and of the empirical flux of transitions. As an application of this general framework, we derive explicit general bounds on the fluctuations of trajectory observables, generalising to the non-Markovian case both thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations. We illustrate our theory with simple examples, and discuss potential applications of these results.

items.title: A Quasipolynomial Algorithm for $\ell_\infty$ Contractions
items.summary: We give an algorithm for computing an $\eps$-approximate fixed point of any $d$-dimensional nonexpansion with respect to the $\ell_\infty$ norm in time $\log(1/\eps)^{O(\log^2 d)}$. At its core, our method uses a boosting argument to geometrically shrink a search region. Among other consequences, our algorithm implies that simple stochastic games can be solved in quasipolynomial time.

items.title: Self-normalized Bernstein Inequalities for Regenerative Processes and Applications to Learning Without Independence
items.summary: We prove a self-normalized Bernstein inequality for bounded functions of a regenerative process with independent, identically distributed marked cycles of finite mean length. The bound uses observed cycle lengths and retains explicit terms for truncation and the cycle ending after the observation horizon. Selecting a tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives a version of Bernstein inequality where all terms are empirical but one, related to the tails of the regeneration times. We then study this term in many regimes: it turns out that it is of second-order in many cases of interest. This is important for applications in machine learning: we prove generalization error bounds for classification with non-i.i.d., regenerative data. These bounds can be used to define learning objectives: by minimizing the first-order term only in the bound, we define agnostic classifiers that still satisfy oracle inequalities. We also show that the bound on the average deviation provided by our results is minimax-optimal in the sample size and in the expected regeneration time. Finally, we combine the Bernstein inequality with a regenerative strong approximation to obtain a Gaussian approximation using an observable block variance estimator.

items.title: On ABP Estimates for a Class of Fully Nonlinear Singular-Degenerate Elliptic Equations and Applications
items.summary: We establish an Alexandrov-Bakelman-Pucci type estimate for a class of fully nonlinear elliptic equations with singular or degenerate coefficients and nonlinear dependence on the gradient. The estimate bounds sub-solutions in terms of their boundary values and weighted integrals of the data. It holds for classical sub-solutions and for viscosity sub-solutions with locally Lipschitz gradients. The assumptions allow general rates of growth in the gradient, with a smallness condition on the data when the associated gradient weight has finite integral. The proof uses the classical weighted contact-set argument. As applications, we obtain sup-norm estimates for viscosity sub-solutions to a class of generalized Monge-Ampère equations, Hessian equations, Hessian quotients under an additional condition on the contact Hessian, and anisotropic mean-curvature-type equations.

items.title: Boundary-Driven Nonequilibrium for the Coulomb Landau Equation
items.summary: We establish a nonlinear theory of the Coulomb Landau equation in smooth bounded domains with non-isothermal diffuse reflection. We construct a stationary state, prove its perturbative uniqueness and global nonlinear stability, and establish exponential convergence when the wall temperature approaches its stationary profile exponentially. We also establish stationary and global nonlinear well-posedness for prescribed inflow, together with asymptotic stability. The analysis combines a critical kinetic integrability gain with finite-exponent velocity-gradient estimates near grazing, allowing the nonlinear Coulomb estimates to close without $L_x^\infty$ control of velocity gradients.

items.title: Minimax Optimality of the NPMLE for Gaussian Mixtures in Hellinger Distance
items.summary: We analyze the problem of estimating univariate Gaussian mixture densities using the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) based on $n$ independent and identically distributed samples. We show that the unconstrained NPMLE achieves the minimax optimal rate $\log(n)/n$ in squared Hellinger distance, when the true mixing measure is sub-Gaussian. In addition, we show that when the true mixing measure has compact support, the NMPLE constrained to a compact interval also achieves the minimax optimal rate, which is slightly faster and of order $\log(n)/(n \log \log n)$. Our proof consists of sharply characterizing the local Hellinger bracketing entropy of the class of finite Gaussian mixtures. One of our key technical innovations is to sharply bound the $L^2$ bracketing entropy of balls of bounded-degree polynomials, which may be of independent interest. As an application, we establish the regret-optimality of $g$-modeling procedures based on the NPMLE in the Gaussian Empirical Bayes problem with bounded priors.

items.title: Certified Decisions
items.summary: Hypothesis tests and confidence sets are ubiquitous in empirical research, yet their connection to subsequent decision-making is often unclear. We view statistical inference as pairing recommended decisions with guarantees of their quality---or certificates---and develop a theory of certified decisions. Specifically, we attach P-certificates---upper bounds on loss that hold with probability at least $1-α$---to recommended actions. We prove that it is without loss to limit attention to P-certificates generated by minimax decisions over confidence sets, or what Manski (2021) terms "as-if decisions with a set estimate." We further show that such certificates allow safe adoption decisions for ambiguity-averse downstream decision-makers. A parallel argument applies to E-certified decisions obtained from e-values in settings with unbounded loss. We illustrate this view of statistical inference through an application to economic mobility and one to AI model routing.

items.title: A nontopological triangulated category which is $θ$-dg enhanced
items.summary: For every nonzero commutative ring $R$ and infinite cardinal $θ$, we construct a nontopological triangulated category over $R$, whose thick subcategories generated by $<θ$ objects admit $R$-linear dg enhancements, while the scalar action of $R$ is faithful.

items.title: A well-posedness theory for the 2D inhomogeneous incompressible Euler equations and a class of global-in-time solutions
items.summary: We consider the Cauchy problem for the 2D inhomogeneous incompressible Euler equations. We show that the Cauchy problem is locally well-posed in a class of $m$-fold symmetric functions at critical regularity and allowing the velocity field to grow linearly at spatial infinity. This was a problem posed by P.L. Lions in the homogeneous, not necessarily symmetric case. A key ingredient is a variable-coefficient elliptic theory developed using quasiconformal mappings and Schauder estimates in certain scale-invariant Hölder spaces. Local well-posedness allows us to derive the one-dimensional system on $\mathbb{S}^1$ satisfied by solutions with $0$-homogeneous vorticity and density. For this system, we can obtain global well-posedness for a class of initial data away from equilibrium. We are unaware of any previous nonperturbative class of time-dependent solutions to the two-dimensional inhomogeneous Euler equations for which global well-posedness has been established. Finally, for some signed global solutions, we show a dichotomy between density homogenization and averaged relaxation in infinite time.

items.title: $SU(2)$ Yang-Mills-Higgs functional with Higgs self-interaction on $3$-manifolds
items.summary:

When $M$ is closed, we use a $3$-parameter min-max construction to produce, for $\varepsilon\ll_M 1$, non-trivial critical points in the energy regime \[ 1 \lesssim_λ\varepsilon^{-1}\mathcal{Y}_{\varepsilon}(

Finally, the estimates involved also lead to an energy gap for critical points on $3$-manifolds with bounded geometry. As a byproduct of our results, we deduce the existence of non-trivial $\mathcal{Y}_{1}$-critical points over $\mathbb{R}^3$ for any $λ>0$.

items.title: On one-dimensional pressureless Euler--Poisson systems: existence for non-semiconvex interaction potentials
items.summary: One-dimensional Euler-Poisson-type systems with interaction potentials that are repulsive at short range and attractive at long range are useful simplified models that describe biological aggregation. In the current work we employ new techniques to treat compactly supported solutions in the case where the potential is $C^1$ and satisfies certain coercivity growth conditions although it is not necessarily semiconvex, as required in previous work. Central to this approach are uniform bounds on the positions and velocities of discrete sticky-particle solutions to such a system, which requires the potential be only $C^{0, 1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. In the semiconvex case, these bounds also yield convergence of time-shifted trajectories to an eternal solution. The tradeoff, just as in the case of repulsive Euler-Poisson, is that we cannot claim that the emerging solutions for non-semiconvex potentials are sticky.

items.title: Distinguishing graphs with simple spectrum by homomorphism counts
items.summary: We study which graph classes determine every graph with simple spectrum up to isomorphism by homomorphism counts from their members. We show that such a class has unbounded treewidth and Euler genus and contains a graph with the complete graph on seven vertices as a minor. To prove these conditions, we construct pairs of non-isomorphic cospectral graphs with simple spectrum, each bipartite, nonsingular and of maximum degree at most six. The construction attaches rooted trees to Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs and preserves homomorphism indistinguishability over every minor-closed class. We then prove that subcubic homomorphism counts determine every graph whose adjacency matrix has kernel dimension at most one. This extends the known result for nonsingular graphs and applies to all graphs with simple spectrum. We also prove that two graphs have the same subcubic homomorphism counts if and only if they have the same number of vertices and there is a bijective linear isometry between the images of their adjacency matrices that intertwines the adjacency operators and preserves the coordinatewise trilinear forms. Finally, we prove that homomorphism counts from the single-vertex graph and from subdivisions of any sequence of connected cubic graphs have the same distinguishing power as subcubic homomorphism counts if every complete graph is a minor of some member of the sequence.

items.title: Joint Uniform Continuity of Reduced Free Products for strong convergence
items.summary: We investigate a generalization of Skoufranis' theorem on joint continuity of free products of laws in the strong topology. Namely, we show that this operation is moreover \emph{uniformly continuous}. Our methods follows those of Piser and go through the estimates of Ricard-Xu.

items.title: When Standardization Spreads Factor Variation Across the Spectrum
items.summary: Standardizing variables by their sample standard deviations is routine in multivariate analysis and removes marginal scale differences before dependence is assessed. The resulting correlation matrix captures both dominant common components and dependence beyond them. A central inferential difficulty arises because the same random sample variances normalize the entire spectrum. In spiked covariance models, the sampling errors of leading and residual eigenvalues can become asymptotically independent. Sample standardization fundamentally changes this behavior and can preserve their dependence, allowing strong factors to remain a major source of uncertainty even after the leading eigenvalues are excluded. To obtain valid inference for both residual and full spectrum statistics, we establish their joint sampling law for sample correlation matrices with diverging spikes. The theory reveals exact trace compensation and statistic dependent transitions between asymptotic independence and dependence as the spikes grow. It leads to tests of an identity correlation matrix under strong factors and a feasible two sample comparison of residual spectral concentration. A sex balanced HapMap analysis illustrates the substantial effect of factor variation on residual spectrum inference.

items.title: AnyonWiki.org
items.summary: The AnyonWiki is an open-source project that provides full algebraic and numerical data of fusion and unitary modular fusion categories as a resource for the scientific community. It comes with a database, the AnyonWikiDatabase, that currently includes the classification of multiplicity-free pivotal (braided) fusion categories through rank 7 and more than 25000 fusion rings including the classification of multiplicity-free fusion rings through rank 10, with work in progress to expand. This data is available through AnyonWiki.org, a website that provides robust search and download functionality and presents each fusion ring and category via a dedicated webpage. In this short article we discuss the data available at AnyonWiki.org as well as the scientific and communal motivations for the design of its underlying AnyonWikiDatabase, which are centered around making the data accessible, independently verifiable, granularly citable, useful, and easy to work with.

items.title: The Dynamics of RMSProp Beyond the Stability Threshold
items.summary: We study what happens to RMSProp when the learning rate is too large for convergence to the minimizer. For positive-definite quadratic loss functions, we show that the minimizer is Lyapunov un- stable above an explicit critical learning rate. Nevertheless, every trajectory eventually enters a compact trapping region. We obtain explicit bounds proportional to h in the spatial variables and to h2 in the memory variables, where h is the learning rate. We also prove that nontrivial period-two orbits exist precisely above the critical learning rate, and under additional spectral assumptions, an attracting branch of these orbits emerges from the minimizer. For sufficiently large learning rates, we construct branches near admissible corners of a cube. We then explore the dynamics inside the trapping region using the parameterization method and numerical continuation, exploring invariant circles and tori, coexistence of attracting sets, circle-doubling sequences, and chaotic motions. We examine how the dynamics depend on the loss Hessian, memory decay, and dimension. Finally, we test a learning-rate reduction schedule and continue selected invariant circles into an autonomous variant of the Adam optimizer.

items.title: Reconstruction of Fano manifolds from the orthogonal to an exceptional coherent sheaf
items.summary: Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth complex Fano manifolds of dimension at least three with very ample anticanonical bundles, and let $\mathcal{E}_X$ and $\mathcal{E}_Y$ be exceptional coherent sheaves on $X$ and $Y$, respectively. We prove that a Fourier--Mukai equivalence $\mathcal{E}_X^\perp\simeq \mathcal{E}_Y^\perp$ implies $X\simeq Y$.

items.title: A linear, second-order, unconditionally energy-stable scalar-auxiliary-variable scheme for the CHQ viscoelastic phase-separation model
items.summary: The CHQ model describes viscoelastic phase separation in a polymer--solvent mixture: a Cahn--Hilliard equation for the polymer volume fraction $φ$ is two-way coupled, through a phase-dependent cross-diffusion flux, to a damped relaxation equation for a scalar bulk elastic stress $q$. We propose a scalar-auxiliary-variable (SAV) time discretisation of this system, combining the SAV reformulation of the double-well potential with a second-order backward differentiation formula (BDF2) and a second-order extrapolation of all phase-dependent mobilities: a linear, computationally cheaper complement to the reference scheme's fully nonlinear Newton solve. The resulting method is (i) linear at every time step, with a coupling structure we prove has exactly one solution at every step, for every choice of time-step size; (ii) mass conserving, exactly, as an algebraic identity of the discrete equations themselves (the only drift ever seen numerically traces to the finite tolerance of the iterative linear solver, not a failure of the conservation property); and (iii) unconditionally stable for a modified discrete energy, via an exact one-step energy--dissipation identity. We show the energy identity extends to this filtered variant as well, with two explicit extra non-negative terms. Hence, the scheme actually producing the physics results is itself provably stable for the same energy. A Fourier--Galerkin implementation verifies that the energy identity holds at every time step to within floating-point round-off. It also confirms second-order temporal accuracy, including in the steep-interface regime, and agreement with an independently implemented nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver. Compared with that independent nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver, at equal grid resolution, the SAV method uses $2.5$--$3.0\times$ fewer linear-solver iterations and $1.7$--$2.0\times$ less wall-clock time.

items.title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
items.summary: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/χ_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $χ_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.

items.title: When Windowed Anderson Acceleration Converges Faster
items.summary: Windowed Anderson acceleration AA($m$) combines at most $m+1$ recent iterates by least squares. For a real affine contraction $x\mapsto Wx+b$ with $q=\|W\| \in(0,1)$, we determine exactly when AA($m$) converges from every starting point with an asymptotic factor below $q$. We give a polynomial criterion for this improvement and an equivalent spectral condition: there is no probability distribution on the phases of the eigenvalues of modulus $q$ whose first $m$ cosine moments are $q,q^2,\ldots,q^m$. If such a distribution exists, we construct a starting point from which AA($m$) reproduces fixed-point iteration at every step. Otherwise, over a fixed number of consecutive steps, every run contracts the residual norm by a common factor strictly smaller than the corresponding power of $q$. The polynomial criterion also gives explicit convergence-rate bounds with constants independent of the dimension. When $q$ equals the spectral radius, this characterizes improvement over the asymptotic convergence factor of fixed-point iteration. For general affine contractions, the asymptotic factor never exceeds the numerical radius of $W$, and a related moment condition gives a uniform upper bound strictly below that radius.

items.title: Domination polynomial of co-maximal graphs of integer modulo ring
items.summary: We investigate the domination polynomial of the co-maximal graph $Γ(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ related to the ring of integers modulo $n$. Such a polynomial encodes domination sets of all possible sizes, a NP-hard problem for general graph. We give exact formulas for prime powers, integers with two distinct prime divisors, and products of three distinct primes. A prime-support decomposition gives a finite explicit formula for arbitrary $n$, including repeated prime factors. Further results determine the highest coefficients, the precise threshold beyond which every vertex subset dominates, and the number of non-dominating subsets. We discuss unimodality and log-concavity, and derive justified bounds for nonzero domination roots using the Eneström--Kakeya theorem.

items.title: Alternative moduli of twisted curves
items.summary: We define new Artin stack compactifications of the moduli of smooth curves, which parameterize "relatively polarized curves" consisting of stacky semistable curves equipped with line bundles that are trivialized away from the rational bridges. Using techniques from birational geometry, we prove that stacks of relatively polarized curves admit the classical coarse space $\overline{M}_g$ of stable curves as a good moduli space. One of our main motivations is a companion paper where we construct a proper moduli space of $\mathrm{SL}_N$-bundles on relatively polarized curves. This suggests the hypothesis that relatively polarized curves are suitable sources for defining Gromov-Witten theory for Artin stack targets.

items.title: Reflection functors for non-simply-laced quiver varieties
