We prove the reductions and pruning conditions,describe the exact storage scheme, and provide source code, execution logs,and a reproduction driver. The result is a computer-assisted proof for thespecified instance, with an explicit implementation trust boundary.

items.title: Normal forms of elliptic automorphic Lie algebras and Landau-Lifshitz type of equations
items.summary: We present normal forms of elliptic automorphic Lie algebras with dihedral symmetry of order 4, which arise naturally in the context of Landau-Lifshitz type of equations. These normal forms provide a transparent description and allow a classification of such Lie algebras over $\mathbb{C}$. Using this perspective, we show that a Lie algebra introduced by Uglov, as well as the hidden symmetry algebra of the Landau-Lifshitz equation introduced by Holod, can each be realised as an elliptic $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$-current algebra. Furthermore, we realise the Wahlquist-Estabrook algebra of the Landau-Lifshitz equation in terms of elliptic automorphic Lie algebras. This construction reveals that, as a complex Lie algebra, it is isomorphic to the direct sum of an $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$-current algebra and the two-dimensional abelian Lie algebra $\mathbb{C}^2$. Finally, we apply the automorphic Lie algebra framework to an $n$-component generalisation of the Landau-Lifshitz equation due to Golubchik and Sokolov in the case $n=3$.

items.title: $q$-middle Laplace transform and its applications
items.summary: We introduce a $q$-analog of the one-variable middle Laplace transform defined by the first author. We establish its invertibility and preservation of irreducibility, and derive a decomposition of $q$-middle convolution in terms of this transform. As applications, we obtain integral representations of solutions to the confluent $q$-hypergeometric equation and its variant, and construct a transformation of the $2\times 2$ Lax linear equation associated with the $q$-Painlevé equation of type $A_4^{(1)}$.

items.title: Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective
items.summary: These lecture notes present an introduction to large deviations in stochastic dynamical systems, adapted from a lecture series given at the Les Houches school ``Large Deviations: Theory and Applications'' in July 2024. The exposition develops the theory through a unified methodology: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations, which reveals the Hamiltonian structure underlying all large deviation principles considered here. We treat three asymptotic regimes systematically. First, the small-noise limit for stochastic differential equations and the large-volume limit for Markov jump processes, where the Large Deviation Principle emerges from the Law of Large Numbers through progressively finer characterizations of fluctuations. Second, the long-time limit combined with small noise, yielding the quasipotential formalism for metastability and transition rates in both equilibrium and nonequlibrium systems. Third, the long-time limit at finite noise, connecting to spectral methods via tilted generators and enabling reduction of multiscale systems. We survey computational approaches including minimum action methods, their geometric variants for quasipotential calculations, and neural network techniques. The Schlögl model of chemical bistability serves as a running example, illustrating both scalar and spatially extended settings. Appendices provide self-contained background on stochastic calculus and Markov jump processes.

items.title: Norms of the Hilbert Matrix Operator on Some Analytic Function Spaces
items.summary: For $\mathcal H:\mathcal B^α\to\mathcal B^α$ with $1<α<2$, we obtain an exact norm representation. In particular, the norm is given by an explicit Gamma-function formula for $1<α\leq3/2$, whereas for $3/2<α<2$ it strictly exceeds the corresponding Gamma-function expression. For $\mathcal H:\mathcal B^α\to\mathcal B^α_{\log}$, we determine the exact norm: it is equal to $3/2$ for $1<α\leq4/3$ and is given by an explicit Gamma-function formula for $4/3<α<2$. We also determine the exact norm of $\mathcal H:H^1\to H^1_{\log}$ and show that it is equal to $π$. Finally, for $0<α<1$, we determine the exact norm of $\mathcal H:H^\infty_α\to\mathcal B^{α+1}$, which is given by an explicit Gamma-function formula.

items.title: Scalar--Mean Rigidity for Hyperbolic Balls in Dimensions $2\le n\le 5$
items.summary: In this paper, we prove the non-spin hyperbolic scalar--mean rigidity theorem in dimensions $2\leq n\leq5$, resolving the corresponding low-dimensional case of a problem of Gromov. The proof combines the Jang deformation with capillary $μ$-bubble dimension reduction. We also establish weighted scalar--mean rigidity for Euclidean ball--torus products in total dimension at most seven and show that its hyperbolic analogue fails.

items.title: Extreme change-point detection
items.summary: We examine rules for predicting whether a point in $\mathbb{R}$ generated from a 50-50 mixture of two different probability distributions came from one distribution or the other, given limited (or no) information on the two distributions, and, as clues, one point generated randomly from each of the two distributions. We prove that nearest-neighbor prediction does better than chance when we know the two distributions are Gaussian densities without knowing their parameter values. We conjecture that this result holds for general probability distributions and, furthermore, that the nearest-neighbor rule is optimal in this setting, i.e., no other rule can do better than it if we do not know the distributions or do not know their parameters, or both.

items.title: Frequency Structure of AMM Liquidity Pools: A Multiresolution Analysis of Regime Transitions
items.summary: This study examines the temporal structure of liquidity pools in constant-product automated market makers. Using a sample of eighteen pools observed at a five-minute frequency over two years, it aims to identify the temporal scales at which interactions within the system occur and how these interactions reorganize in response to changes in the volatility regime. Methodologically, the study proposes a strictly causal Haar multiresolution analysis in which each variable is estimated using only the information available at the time of measurement. Within this decomposition, three dimensions are examined: the scale composition of the return-to-risk relationship, the frequency-band coupling between pool activity and price volatility, and the detection of regime transitions using a fluctuation-to-trend indicator. The results reveal a clear structural segmentation: pool variability is concentrated at fast scales, whereas the relationships among its series, signal persistence, and information on subsequent performance reside at slow scales. Aggregate measures do not distinguish this separation because they combine both components before they can be compared.

items.title: Local Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture for unitary groups: Trace formula approach for epsilon dichotomy
items.summary: The purpose of this paper is to provide a proof independent of the theta-lifting for the epsilon-dichotomy of the local Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture of real unitary groups for tempered L-parameters. The approach is based on the local trace formula and endoscopic character identities following Waldspurger and Chen-Luo.

items.title: Symmetry Inheritance and Exact Mirror Symmetry Reduction for Electric Field Vector Wave Problems with PEC Boundaries
items.summary: A symmetry-inheritance and exact domain-reduction framework is developed for the second-order vector wave equation of the electric field in bounded domains with a perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary and general spatially varying anisotropic media. Orthogonal group actions on polar vectors, axial vectors, and second-order constitutive tensors are used to derive the transformed curl--curl equation and PEC trace directly from the original boundary-value problem. Under unique solvability, the common symmetry group of the problem data is inherited by the electric field. When the symmetry group of the electromagnetic medium admits a mirror symmetry, an arbitrary impressed current can be decomposed by the associated reflection projectors into mirror-even and mirror-odd components. The corresponding full-domain fields inherit the respective parities, and their exact restriction to one half-domain yields a perfect magnetic conductor (PMC) condition for the even field and a PEC condition for the odd field. The original problem is therefore represented exactly by two independent reduced-domain problems. A symmetry-compatible first-family Nédélec discretization preserves this decomposition at the discrete level. Analytical and numerical results verify the symmetry-inheritance theory, the exact PEC/PMC reduced-domain formulations, and the discrete reconstruction for constant and spatially varying anisotropic conductive media under both symmetric and asymmetric excitations.

items.title: Revisiting the infinite Galois correspondence via group representations
items.summary: Inspired by Lenstra's infinite normal basis theorem, we interpret the Galois correspondence as a special case of a simple general principle in harmonic analysis on profinite groups. This also gives a representation-theoretic characterisation of profinite groups.

items.title: The Sample Complexity of Multiple Change Point Identification under Bandit Feedback
items.summary: We study multiple change point localization under bandit feedback. An unknown piecewise-constant function on a compact interval can be queried sequentially at adaptively chosen inputs, and each query returns a noisy evaluation of the function. The goal is to identify a prescribed number of discontinuities, known as change points, within a target precision $η$ and confidence level $1-δ$, while using as few samples as possible. We propose an adaptive algorithm that first detects intervals likely to contain change points and then refines their locations to precision $η$. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds on its sample budget, together with corresponding lower bounds. Prior work shows that jump magnitudes alone determine the asymptotic sample complexity as $δ\to 0$. We reveal that this picture is incomplete beyond this regime. We demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that for general $δ$ and $η$, the complexity is jointly governed by the jumps and the relative positions of the change points.

items.title: Density-Level Backward Error for Low-NFE Generative Flows
items.summary: Low-NFE generative ODE sampling is constrained not only by solver order, but also by how a fixed budget of network evaluations is distributed along the flow. We develop a density-level backward-error framework that identifies the component of a solver's modified-equation defect that changes the evolving marginal, while excluding solenoidal trajectory distortion that is invisible in Wasserstein tangent geometry. The resulting residual induces a solver-order-aware compute-allocation rule and, through gauge freedom, an objective for selecting numerically favorable velocity representatives of the same density path. This separates our approach from schedule search driven by trajectory or endpoint surrogates and from higher-order solver design. Exact Gaussian and mixture models establish the mechanism, including cases where curvature-based allocation fails and continuum-optimal transport is not discretization-optimal. On a pretrained CIFAR-10 EDM probability-flow ODE, density-aware allocation consistently improves fixed-update Euler sampling in the low-NFE regime. Matched-seed convergence to a dense Euler reference confirms that the method accelerates approximation of the same high-NFE flow rather than changing the asymptotic sampler.

items.title: The Follow-the-Leader scheme with non-monotone velocity
items.summary: This paper addresses the approximation of entropy solutions to a one-dimensional scalar conservation law via the so-called Follow-the-Leader particle scheme in case the velocity map is \emph{non monotone}. The result is based on a discrete maximum principle, on $BV$ estimates of the approximated density, and on the characterization of the limit as entropy solution in the sense of Kru\v zkov.

items.title: Weights and characters for affine Hecke algebras
items.summary: Weights play an essential role in the classification of simple modules for affine Hecke algebras. In this paper we show the extent to which weights determine simple modules and relate this to induction and restriction along isogenies. We also describe the behaviour of hermitian duals and unitarity under induction and restriction along isogenies.

items.title: Enhanced Langlands Parameters of Regular Principal Series
items.summary: We describe the enhanced Langlands parameters of the irreducible constituents of a regular principal series of a quasi-split reductive group over a non-archimedean local field of characteristic zero. Starting from the chamber parametrization by Rodier and Luo, we determine the monodromy of each constituent and show that its enhancement is trivial. In particular, we obtain the corresponding parameter of the unique irreducible subrepresentation.

items.title: The exceptional set of Goldbach numbers within the set of squares
items.summary: We prove that the set of numbers of type $n = 2m^2$ below $X$ which cannot be written as a sum of two primes has cardinality at most $X^{19/24 + o(1)}$.

items.title: An entropy proof of the commonality of apices of trees
items.summary: A graph $H$ is called common if the number of monochromatic copies of $H$ in a $2$-edge-colouring of a large complete graph is asymptotically minimized by the random colouring with an equal proportion of each colour. Grzesik, Lee, Lidický and Volec conjectured that every $k$-apex of any connected Sidorenko graph is common. Recently, Kr{á}l', Krnc and Lamaison proved that the $k$-apex of any tree is common for $k\leq 5$. In this paper, we extend their result by showing that for every positive integer $k$, the $k$-apex of any tree or any forest with average degree at least one is common. Our proof involves an application of the entropy method.

items.title: General function bases moment models for suspended sediment with vertical profile of concentration
items.summary: We introduce a general hydrostatic shallow moment framework for suspended sediment transport with vertically varying horizontal velocity and concentration profiles. The formulation is constructed over arbitrary vertical functional bases that are numerically orthogonalised via the Gram-Schmidt algorithm. This approach allows the approximation spaces for the vertical profile to be adapted to the specific structure of each physical variable, where also the velocity and sediment concentration can be projected onto different functional spaces. To overcome the limitations due to the inherent oscillatory nature of global Legendre polynomials, we explore a specific continuous piecewise linear $\mathbb{P}_1$ finite-element basis. Furthermore, non-uniform vertical partitions are considered, enabling an enhanced representation of the vertical profiles in specific regions. Numerical experiments involving boundary layers and suspended sediment transport demonstrate that the proposed framework is accurate to reproduce the expected vertical profiles. The improvement is particularly significant for sediment concentration profiles with sharp vertical variations, where polynomial reconstructions exhibit pronounced oscillations leading to physically meaningless profiles, whereas the $\mathbb{P}_1$ bases produce a qualitatively accurate representation of the vertical profiles observed in the sedimentation processes.

items.title: Approximate Matrix Multiplication through Joint Leverage Score Sampling
items.summary: In this paper, we investigate approximate matrix multiplication through random sampling. Specifically, we propose using a non-uniform sampling distribution constructed from the leverage scores of the two matrices, and characterize the associated approximation error in terms of the matrix spectral norm; which is well-known to better characterize the downstream error when the matrix product operator is applied to an input vector. We provide the probability error bounds for the proposed algorithm are also given, and discuss connections to data-oblivious approximate matrix multiplication, and graph sparsification algorithms.

items.title: Local well-posedness, blow-up phenomenon and ill-posedness for a model system of the radiating gas
items.summary: In this paper, we investigate the Cauchy problem for a model system of radiating gas in multi-dimensional space. Firstly, we prove that the model is locally well-posed in Besov spaces $B^s_{p,r}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $s>1+\frac{d}{p}$ (resp., $s=1+\frac{d}{p}$, $r=1$), including the endpoint space $B^1_{\infty,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Secondly, we show that the data-to-solution map is not uniformly continuous on bounded subsets of these Besov spaces. Moreover, we construct a blow-up scenario and derive two sufficient blow-up conditions, which improve the previous blow-up condition obtained in \cite{MR3016436}. Finally, we prove that the Cauchy problem is ill-posed in the critical space $B^{1+\frac{d}{p}}_{p,r}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $1\leq p\leq\infty$ and $r>1$ in the sense of norm inflation.

items.title: Absolute continuity of the law of the solution to the stochastic Cahn-Hilliard equation driven by fractional noise
items.summary: The stochastic partial differential equation analyzed in this work is the Cahn-Hilliard equation perturbed by an additive fractional white noise (fractional in time and white in space). We work in spatial dimensions $d \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ with $d < 4H$, where $H \in (\frac{1}{2}, 1)$ is the Hurst parameter of the noise, and apply Malliavin calculus to investigate the existence of a density for the solution $u$. In particular, we show that $u$ admits a jointly continuous modification and construct a localizing sequence through which we prove that its Malliavin derivative exists locally, and that its law is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$, thereby establishing that a density exists. We obtain the result for the whole range of dimensions and Hurst parameters in which the mild solution is known to exist. The analysis rests on three new estimates. The first bounds the expectation of the $p$-th power ($p \geq 2$) of the $L^{\infty}(D)$-norm of the stochastic integral appearing in the mild formulation. The other two concern the integral involving the operator associated with the kernel that appears in the integral representation of the fractional noise: an upper estimate and, more importantly, a lower estimate on short time intervals, which yields the nondegeneracy of the Malliavin derivative.

items.title: Cobordism, spin structures, and profinite completions
items.summary: Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth closed connected aspherical manifolds with good (in the sense of Serre) fundamental groups $G$ and $H$. We show that if $\widehat G\cong \widehat H$, then $M$ and $N$ are cobordant and the signatures of $M$ and $N$ agree modulo $8$. Moreover, $M$ is spin (resp. spin$^\mathbb{C}$) if and only if $N$ is spin (resp. spin$^\mathbb{C}$). We consider some analogous results for compact connected aspherical manifolds.

items.title: Galois Groups of Shifted Exponential Polynomials
items.summary: Consider the shifted truncations of the exponential series and their Galois groups: $$F_{n,a}(x) := \sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{x^j}{(a+j)!}\qquad G_{n,a}:= \text{Gal}(F_{n,a}/\mathbb{Q}).$$ In this paper we prove that for every fixed integer $a>0$, the set of $n$ for which $G_{n,a}=S_n$ has natural density one, thus answering a question of Katz and Rivin.

items.title: Commutative algebras satisfying univariate identities with vanishing Peirce polynomial
items.summary: This paper introduces and studies $(2,3)$-palintropic algebras, a class of commutative algebras defined by the identity $(x^{2})^3 - (x^{3})^2 = 0$. This specific relation is the simplest generator of the $2$-dimensional space of minimal-degree evanescent identities in degree $6$, and encompasses several well-studied structures, including Jordan and medial algebras. The primary motivation for investigating these algebras lies in their trivial Peirce polynomials, which removes a priori restrictions on the spectrum of the multiplication operator associated with an idempotent. This paper reviews and further develops the theory of Peirce operators, Peirce polynomials, and second-order linearizations. It shows that despite the triviality of the Peirce polynomial, any idempotent $c$ admits well-behaved, explicit fusion rules for multiplication between its $λ$-Peirce spaces for $λ\neq \tfrac{1}{2}$. Furthermore, multiplication by a nonsingular idempotent is an algebra homomorphism. Finally, there are given concrete examples of $(2,3)$-palintropic algebras, together with applications of these algebraic structures to commutative polynomial maps.

items.title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials
items.summary: Significant spatial heterogeneity and nonlocal history-dependent attenuation jointly govern wave propagation in composite materials, making full-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) computationally prohibitive. This study proposed a high-order multi-scale (HOMS) method for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems with highly oscillatory and discontinuous material coefficients. Using a multi-scale asymptotic expansion approach, the macroscopic homogenized equation, and first- and second-order correction terms are derived to construct the high-accuracy HOMS solution. Moreover, a local pointwise error analysis identifies the leading residual eliminated by this HOMS solution and validates its local physical balance preservation. Then, a global energy-norm error estimate establishes the $O(\varepsilon)$-order convergence rate for the HOMS solution. Subsequently, an efficient spatiotemporal multi-scale algorithm integrating the finite element and finite difference methods is designed, which employs a novel fully discrete $L2\text{-}1_σ$-Newmark scheme, and corresponding unconditional shifted-energy stability and explicit convergence rates are also obtained for the macroscopic homogenized displacement and velocity, respectively. Both two- and three-dimensional examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, reduced cost, and robustness of the proposed HOMS method. This work provides an effective multi-scale tool for nonlocal-in-time wave simulation in engineering applications.

items.title: Computing Theta Characteristics and their Galois action on general curves of moderate genus
items.summary: In this article, we present an algorithm that, given a smooth curve $X$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, returns an explicit arithmetic representation of both odd and even Theta Characteristics split by parity. It allows us to retrieve their Galois action and étale algebra. The output includes the Theta Hyperplanes of the Theta Characteristics when they are finite, their associated proof functions as well as the dictionary of their quadratic forms. The algorithm works in a rather large generality as it handles any one-equation (potentially singular) model of smooth curves. The most binding requirement remains the necessity for an explicit degree 1 rational divisor on the curve or more likely a rational point. We implemented the algorithm and give examples up to genus $5$.

items.title: Classification of analytic conformal product structures
items.summary: We classify real-analytic conformal product structures on compact simply connected manifolds in all dimensions $n\ge 2$. We prove that in dimension $2$ and $3$ no such structure exists, while in every dimension $n\ge 4$ the two parallel distributions arise from a global product splitting.

items.title: A Dehornoy-Type Ordering on Bridge Positions of Links
items.summary: By a theorem of Hovland, bridge isotopy classes of $n$-bridge positions of links in $S^3$ correspond bijectively to Hilden double cosets $P_{2n}=H_{2n}\backslash B_{2n}/H_{2n}$. We use this correspondence to introduce Dehornoy-type orderings on bridge positions. After fixing a proper complexity function on $B_{2n}$, we assign to each double coset its Dehornoy-minimal braid among the elements of minimal complexity. Comparing these representatives by the Dehornoy order gives a strict total order $\prec_{D,n}$, and comparing them first by complexity and then by the Dehornoy order gives a strict well-order $\triangleleft_{D,n}$. For a link type $L$ and $n\geq b(L)$, we single out a canonical $n$-bridge position $\operatorname{CanPlat}_D^{(n)}(L)$: it is the $\triangleleft_{D,n}$-least element of the set of $n$-bridge positions of $L$, and the $\prec_{D,n}$-least element among those of minimal complexity, and its canonical braid coincides with the globally Dehornoy-minimal braid of minimal complexity representing $L$. We show by an example that, in general, it need not be least for $\prec_{D,n}$ on the whole set. Finally, we show that the fixed-level bridge finiteness conjecture is equivalent to boundedness of the complexities of the canonical representatives, and to the existence of a $\triangleleft_{D,n}$-greatest $n$-bridge position.

items.title: Data-Driven Hull-Fouling Cleaning Schedule Optimization to Reduce Carbon Footprint of Vessels
items.summary: In response to climate change, the International Maritime Organization has introduced regulations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping. Compliance with these regulations is increasingly expected from individual shipping companies and can be achieved through more frequent hull and propeller cleanings. Since this maintenance work entails high costs, vessel operators are confronted with the trade-off between lower fleet emissions and better economic performance. As a result, assessing whether fuel efficiency has declined sufficiently to warrant cleaning from an environmental and economic standpoint is a critical task. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel dynamic-programming-based algorithm to optimize vessel cleaning schedules. The main components of the optimization problem are a data-driven function for the fuel consumption costs and an additive term that sums up the costs per vessel cleaning. In numerical experiments, we demonstrate the usefulness of our proposed methodology based on real-world sensor data from nine tramp trading vessels. The results confirm that, over four years, fuel consumption can be reduced by up to 5%, even when accounting for the costs of the additional cleaning events.

items.title: Serre weight conjectures for $\mathrm{GSp}_4$
items.summary: We prove the weight part of Serre's conjecture for Galois representations valued in $\mathrm{GSp}_4$ that are tamely ramified with explicit genericity at places above $p$ as conjectured by Herzig--Tilouine and Gee--Herzig--Savitt. This improves on arXiv:2304.13879 where an inexplicit genericity hypothesis was required. As an application, we prove a modularity lifting theorem for $\mathrm{GSp}_4$ under similar assumptions.

items.title: Normalized solutions to an exponential growth Choquard equation driven by mixed local-nonlocal operator in $\mathbb{R}^2$
items.summary: In this paper, we study the existence of normalized solutions to the mixed nonlinear Choquard equation with exponential growth \begin{equation} \left\{ \mathcal{L}u+λu = Λ(I_α*F(u))f(u) \text{ in }\mathbb{R}^{2}; \;\; \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\,dx = a^{2}, \right. \end{equation} where $\mathcal{L}=-Δ+(-Δ)^s$, $0<s<1$, $a>0$, $I_α$ is the Riesz potential of order $α\in(0,2)$, $Λ>0$, and $λ\in\mathbb{R}$ arises as a Lagrange multiplier. The nonlinearity has critical exponential growth in the sense of the Trudinger-Moser inequality. Using variational methods, the associated Pohožaev manifold, and suitable Moser-type estimates, we establish the existence of a normalized solution of mountain-pass type with associated non zero Lagrange multiplier. Under an additional monotonicity assumption on the nonlinearity, we further show that the obtained solution is a normalized ground state. We also establish the regularity properties required for the proof of the corresponding Pohožaev identity.

items.title: Agentic World Action Models
items.summary: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.

items.title: World of SWECraft: Agent Collaboration at Scale via Simulated Software Worlds
items.summary: As teams of AI agents take on larger projects and long-standing open problems, agent collaboration offers another dimension for scaling inference-time compute. To understand what makes such collaboration effective and scalable, we develop Software World, a framework for simulating multi-agent coworking in realistic software ecosystems. It comes with a pipeline to create environments of real, interdependent Python packages of different topics, sizes, and dependency structures, which we call software worlds. In a simulation, agents maintain packages in the world with a high-level goal of improving software efficiency, and they are free to discover tasks to work on and collaborate with others. We evaluate agents' work in a world collectively by measuring speedup in hidden dependent packages. The framework allows us to study different elements of collaboration by varying communication, ownership, and resource allocation. We run simulations in three different worlds, totaling more than 10,000 hours of agent work across eight models. Overall, performance improvement scales with inference-time compute, with the best model improving downstream efficiency by up to 31%. We show that most agents can find meaningful tasks via collaboration, but some frontier models can prematurely stop looking for improvements and make little progress. We release the simulation framework and traces to support future studies of agent collaboration at https://szj.io/sw.

items.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.

items.title: Triggering Stealthy Feature Map Backdoors via Physical Fault Injection in Embedded Neural Networks
items.summary: Fault injection (FI) attacks on embedded neural network (NN) implementations primarily focus on inducing misclassification by corrupting weights or intermediate computations, overlooking their interaction with algorithmic adversarial threats. In this work, we present a cross-level attack that bridges implementation-level physical faults to algorithm-level adversarial attacks. By characterizing fault-induced data perturbations during NN inference, we connect FI with backdoor learning, enabling system-level attacks that jointly exploit implementation- and algorithm-level vulnerabilities. Specifically, we propose a precise fault-injection method that reliably manipulates targeted register values to tractable states during execution. Leveraging this level of FI precision, we propose a novel end-to-end feature map-level backdoor attack, where physically induced intermediate perturbations serve as stealthy triggers. Unlike conventional input-based backdoors, our trigger is activated only under physical faults, causing the NN to exhibit adversarial behavior that compromises system integrity while remaining benign during normal operation. We demonstrate that such physically triggered backdoors can be mounted on embedded NN platforms and remain effective against existing backdoor defenses that typically assume input-space triggers. We showcase the attack practicality using electromagnetic FI on convolutional neural networks implemented on ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller, which is a common platform for constrained embedded applications. Our results highlight a novel attack vector at the intersection of hardware and algorithmic levels, stressing the need for defenses across abstraction levels.

items.title: Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
items.summary: Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-21-cadre

items.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
items.summary: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

items.title: VoxProg: 3D Spatial Reasoning through Voxel Programming
items.summary: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.

items.title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
items.summary: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.

items.title: ALPS: Visual State Encoders for World Models
items.summary: World models turn visual representations into predictions and actions. We argue that their visual foundation should combine physical-state information, native language alignment, and pixel reconstruction, so that a single representation can support prediction, instruction, and inspection. However, existing encoders typically specialize in only one or two of these capabilities; we therefore introduce ALPS, a pretrained visual state encoder that unifies all three in a single set of patch tokens. Using only still images and text, we pretrain a ViT-B/16 from scratch with language, reconstruction, and spatial correspondence objectives, and then refine it via cross-view self-distillation. In a unified evaluation across fifteen public encoders, ALPS achieves the lowest aggregate LIBERO state-probe error among ViT-B models (matching the 3.5x larger V-JEPA 2-L) while maintaining strong language alignment and accurate pixel reconstruction. Downstream, frozen ALPS tokens reach the highest mean policy success on LIBERO (85.5%) when paired with our native text tower, match or exceed leading encoders on world-model planning across PushT, Wall, and Granular, and allow predicted future tokens to be decoded directly into pixels for visual inspection. We hope this work helps establish visual pretraining as a shared foundation for understanding, prediction, and action in world models.

items.title: The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks
items.summary: The success of convolutional neural networks is often attributed to locality and weight sharing. However, how these two properties separately shape learning, and how their effects depend on the spatial correlations of natural images, remain poorly understood. We address these questions in a teacher-student model with a convolutional teacher acting on $P$ input positions with correlation $c$ between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension $D$. For uncorrelated positions ($c = 0$), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly $P$ times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D)$ samples, whereas $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log(D))$ samples are needed with a larger kernel. For $c > 0$, spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with $c$, whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of $c$ and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically.

items.title: CW-WAM: A Structured Contact-Wrench World Action Model for Force-Sensitive Manipulation
items.summary: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively, with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution. Project website: https://cw-wam-project.github.io/

items.title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution
items.summary: Through a tangle of real-world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. Across nine frontier LLMs, solving and authoring prove to be distinct skills: the strongest solvers are not the strongest authors, while smaller models learn more from how others played and write the hardest environments and the most useful hints. Beyond the scores, the pairwise interactions form a microcosm of how models affect one another. Head-to-head outcomes are transitive and so yield a stable ranking; independent authors converge on the same designs; and in a reinforcement-learning study with Qwen3.8-27B, the learner's hint lift on an author's environments tracks how much training on those environments improves it on held-out reasoning and agentic benchmarks, whether the environments are its own or another model's. Each of these patterns has a counterpart in how models shape one another outside the duel. By staging these interactions under controlled conditions, Environment Duels offers a window onto how LLMs teach, challenge and learn from one another. Code is available at https://github.com/LLM-Duels/EnvDuels.

items.title: The End of Consensus Research?
items.summary: Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open, as it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation. We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions. Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads. A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path, selected according to network topology and workload. At the heart of our discovery lies AI-greement, an agent harness for the "autonomous" discovery, implementation, experimentation, and verification of candidate protocols. AI-greement integrates (1) a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base, (2) a modular implementation skeleton, and (3) a Lean-based verification framework with reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proofs. AI-greement is of independent interest: its Lean formalization uncovers several previously unreported vulnerabilities in existing consensus protocols, and it provides guidelines on how domain-specific harnesses can turn general-purpose coding agents into effective tools for (distributed) computing research. Yet we argue that human consensus experts remain essential before, during, and after the search: agents reshape the researcher's role rather than end consensus research.

items.title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research
items.summary: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022--2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.

items.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
items.summary: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

items.title: Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching
items.summary: Flow matching trains a continuum of velocity regression problems but usually reports a loss averaged over interpolation time, obscuring which regions are limited by intrinsic ambiguity and which remain data-limited. We introduce the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP), $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$, the time-local Bayes-risk floor of velocity prediction, and decompose time-resolved loss as $L_N(t)=\mathcal{A}_v(t)+R(t;N)$, where only the excess term $R(t;N)$ is reducible by more data or a different estimator. For $N$ training samples and a $K$-component mixture in the structured example, we prove two statistical benchmarks. In an intrinsic local-regression benchmark, $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$ enters the time-dependent noise factor of the standard nonparametric rate. In separated isotropic Gaussian mixtures, the Bayes velocity becomes locally affine, and a label-oracle residual-regression benchmark has parametric excess-risk scale $K\mathcal{A}_v(t)/N$, matched within the same separated residual Gaussian-location subproblem. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate this diagnostic through a dense transition sweep, calibrated oracle-to-blind and empirical-proxy audits, and a local controlled time-sampler stress test in which a frozen reducible-error proxy reduces reducible loss while cross-cell sensitivity delimits aggressive sampling. On CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature flow, guided time sampling reduces uniformly evaluated velocity loss by $6.78\%$ and global feature Fréchet distance (FD) by $23.6\%$, while class-conditional kernel inception distance (KID) shows no improvement. VAP turns an averaged flow-matching objective into a time-resolved diagnostic for locating ambiguity-limited and data-limited regions.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
items.summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

items.title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
items.summary: Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively. Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses ~100x fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

items.title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard
items.summary: Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes.

items.title: Did the Problem Actually Get Harder? Testing LLMs on Paired P and NP-Complete Problems Hardened by Adversarial Multi-Agent Rewriting
items.summary: Many NP-complete (NPC) problems have a polynomial-time (P) twin that differs in a single structural detail, such as 3- versus 2-colouring a graph. A model that reasons rather than recalls should notice which side of this boundary a problem falls on, yet existing benchmarks either fix the wording of each task or ignore its complexity class, so they cannot separate the two. We introduce P2NPCBench, a benchmark of 12 problem families in which every NPC problem is paired with a P twin posed over the same surface. To remove the textbook cues that enable recall, we build it with AgentGAN, an adversarial multi-agent framework in which a generator rewrites each statement until a panel of frozen code models fails, while an executable validity gate keeps every rewrite answer- and class-preserving. The result is 2,114 hardened statements with hand-verified reference human solvers. Evaluating 12 proprietary and open-source models, we find that every model scores lower on NPC statements than on their P twins (35.4% vs. 63.8% pass@1), and that 95.1% of model-family pairs fail more often on the NPC side. A tenfold time limit raises NPC accuracy only from 28.5% to 31.9%, so failures stem from wrong or crashing programs rather than slow ones. Hardening also narrows the class gap from 24.8 to 14.6 points, showing that part of the apparent gap reflects familiarity with textbook phrasing rather than complexity class.

items.title: Implementation of Dynamic Microsegmentation for a Multi-Robot Network
items.summary: This report describes a laboratory instantiation of a dynamic microsegmentation function for an Internet-of-Things network, specifically a multi-robot network, using a commercial software-defined microsegmentation tool. Fine-grained dynamic segmentation policies are defined, where segments are adapted based on asset functional and health tags. Automated implementation of the dynamic policies in software is also undertaken. The microsegmentation solution is shown to automatically isolate an indicated threat in real time, while maintaining unaffected operations. The demonstration indicates that microsegmentation can be implemented in IoT networks, in a way that allows for robust operation in the face of threats and disruptions.

items.title: $\mathbf{R}^3$: Reconstruction, Raw, and Rain: Deraining Directly in the Bayer Domain
items.summary: Image reconstruction from corrupted images is crucial across many domains. Most reconstruction networks are trained on post-ISP sRGB images, even though the image-signal-processing pipeline irreversibly mixes colors, clips dynamic range, and blurs fine detail. This paper uses the rain degradation problem as a use case to show that these losses are avoidable, and demonstrates that learning directly on raw Bayer mosaics yields superior reconstructions. To substantiate the claim, we (i) evaluate post-ISP and Bayer reconstruction pipelines, (ii) curate Raw-Rain, the first public benchmark of real rainy scenes captured in both 12-bit Bayer and bit-depth-matched sRGB, and (iii) introduce Information Conservation Score (ICS), a color-invariant metric that aligns more closely with human opinion than PSNR or SSIM. On the test split, our raw-domain model improves sRGB results by up to +0.99 dB PSNR and +1.2% ICS, while running faster with half of the GFLOPs. The results advocate an ISP-last paradigm for low-level vision and open the door to end-to-end learnable camera pipelines.

items.title: Building SQL Equivalence Proofs from Query Rewrite Rules
items.summary: Query rewriting and semantic evaluation of text-to-SQL systems both depend on deciding whether two SQL queries return the same result on every database satisfying the schema constraints. Decades of equivalence-preserving optimizer rules provide a natural basis for constructive proofs: two queries are equivalent when admitted rewrites transform them to a common logical expression. Building on this observation, \sys{} organizes query-rewriting knowledge as a standalone proof-producing system. It separates rule validation from proof discovery, explicitly aligns alternative query representations, and returns the resulting rewrite derivation. Across three corpus classes, EquiTrace proves 648/1,106 expected-equivalent text-to-SQL pairs (58.6%), 229/266 curated pairs (86.1%), and 97/240 LLM-generated rewrites whose results agree under benchmark execution (40.4%). On the query rewrite corpus, EquiTrace proves 97 pairs, compared with 35 for QED and 38 for SQLSolver. An analysis of 1,242 recorded proofs shows that coverage depends on a small number of transformations, while many frequently used rules are individually substitutable. The resulting derivations make each proof replayable and expose the specific transformations on which it depends.

items.title: On the Monitorability of Natural Language Autoencoders: Identification vs Discrimination
items.summary: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) are proposed as oversight tools for language models: an Activation Verbaliser (AV) writes an English explanation of an activation vector, and an Activation Reconstructor (AR) maps the explanation back to a vector. Their value for oversight depends on a human monitor being able to tell a true account of an activation from a false one, given the AV's explanation. We formalise NLA training and NLA oversight deployment as two different referential games from Emergent Communication: training is a generative referential game, while oversight is a discriminative, multi-modal, partially-observable referential game played over a many-to-many relation between the monitored language model's activations and the accounts that are true of them. The gap between the two games predicts that AV's explanations will identify which activation they describe without discriminating its true account from closely matched false ones, since training never asks explanations to rule anything out. Using the NLA's own AR as a maximally-sympathetic surrogate monitor model, we experimentally confirm this theoretical insight on one released checkpoint: true accounts beat accounts of other activations in all 320 comparisons, but beat fluent rivals differing in a single claim only 60.2% of the time (standard error 6.7%, chance at 50%, $n = 35$). A meaning-preserving rewrite by an uninvolved model costs only 2.1% of the distance to another activation's account, so the failure is not due to the NLA pair having developed private conventions in the AV's explanations. Our rival accounts test only transcript-level truths, which the monitored language model's conversation settles, so these results bound the easiest case and leave claims about the monitored model's own processing untested. We state conjectures that would make both results consequences of the framework.

items.title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback
items.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient {model size $d$}. Such dependence is prohibitive in modern {overparameterized models} where $d$ is vast. In this work, we study \emph{Private Sparse RLHF} problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^* \ll d$ relevant features. We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings. Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_2$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + {s^*}^2/n^2\varepsilon^2)$ for $(\varepsilon,δ)$-Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + s^*/n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon$-Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP. Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

items.title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

items.title: Exploiting Concavity Information in Gaussian Process Contextual Bandit Optimization
items.summary: The contextual bandit models sequential decision-making problems in which rewards depend on both the chosen action and observed context. In many domains such as medicine, business, and engineering, prior knowledge provides structural information about the reward function that can be exploited to improve optimization efficiency. This paper studies settings where, for each observable context, the conditional mean reward is known to be concave with respect to the action variable. To leverage this structure, we develop a contextual bandit algorithm that conditions a Bayesian Gaussian Process posterior on concavity constraints. We propose a novel reward model that combines a concavity-preserving regression spline basis with a constrained GP posterior, yielding a tractable shape-constrained estimator. Building on this model, we construct a UCB algorithm and establish new posterior concentration inequalities for the constrained posterior, leading to regret guarantees that are never worse than applying standard GP-UCB without concavity information and can be strictly tighter when concavity is informative. Experiments on benchmark problems and a Warfarin dosing test application demonstrate substantial reductions in cumulative regret relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Hyperactive Minority Alters the Stability of Community Notes
items.summary: As platforms increasingly scale down professional fact-checking, community-based alternatives are promoted as more transparent and democratic. The main substitute being proposed is community-based contextualization, most notably Community Notes on X, where users write annotations and collectively rate their helpfulness under a consensus-oriented algorithm. This shift raises a basic empirical question: to what extent do users' social dynamics affect the emergence of Community Notes? We address this question by characterizing participation and political behavior, using the full public release of notes and ratings (between 2021 and 2025). We show that contribution activity is highly concentrated: a small minority of users accounts for a disproportionate share of ratings. Crucially, these high-activity contributors are not neutral volunteers: they are selective in the content they engage with and substantially more politically polarized than the overall contributor population. We replicate the notes' emergence process by integrating the open-source implementation of the Community Notes consensus algorithm used in production. This enables us to conduct counterfactual simulations that modify the display status of notes by varying the pool of raters. Our results reveal that the system is structurally unstable: the emergence and visibility of notes often depend on the behavior of a few dozen highly active users, and even minor perturbations in their participation can lead to markedly different outcomes. In sum, rather than decentralizing epistemic authority, community-based fact-checking on X reconfigures it, concentrating substantial power in the hands of a small, polarized group of highly active contributors.

items.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift
items.summary: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

items.title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video
items.summary: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.

items.title: CanLegalRAGBench: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Canadian Case Law
items.summary: RAG-based legal assistants have been growing in popularity, but LLM hallucinations remain a key issue and potentially undermines justice. While benchmarks have been developed to evaluate progress, many rely on synthetic queries rather than realistic legal scenarios. Moreover, Canadian law remains underrepresented in existing evaluations. To address this gap, we introduce CanLegalRAGBench, a Canadian legal QA benchmark based on realistic queries and expert-annotated answers grounded in case law. Our evaluation shows that retrieval performance is sensitive to design choices and that open-source embedding models are competitive with closed source models. However, it also reveals the limitation of automatic evaluations that penalize systems for retrieving alternative relevant documents. We also find that generated answers often diverge from gold responses, either with hallucinations or by producing overly detailed or irrelevant content, with 8-29% of claims not being supported by the retrieved documents. We hope this benchmark will help drive continued progress in addressing limitations of legal RAG systems.

items.title: Learning Large-Scale Competitive Team Behaviors with Mean-Field Interactions
items.summary: While multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has been proven effective across both collaborative and competitive tasks, existing algorithms often struggle to scale to large populations of agents. Recent advancements in mean-field (MF) theory provide scalable solutions by approximating population interactions as a continuum, yet most existing frameworks focus exclusively on either fully cooperative or purely competitive settings. To bridge this gap, we introduce MF-MAPPO, a mean-field extension of PPO designed for zero-sum team games that integrate intra-team cooperation with inter-team competition. MF-MAPPO employs a shared actor and a minimally informed critic per team and is trained directly on finite-population simulators, thereby enabling deployment to realistic scenarios with thousands of agents. We further show that MF-MAPPO naturally extends to partially observable settings through a simple gradient-regularized training scheme. Our evaluation utilizes large-scale benchmark scenarios using our own testing simulation platform for MF team games (MFEnv), including offense-defense battlefield tasks as well as variants of population-based rock-paper-scissors games that admit analytical solutions, for benchmarking. Across these benchmarks, MF-MAPPO outperforms existing methods and exhibits complex, heterogeneous behaviors, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining mean-field theory and MARL techniques at scale.

items.title: The Best Programming Language for Tokenmaxxing: An Investigation of Coding Agent Behavior Across Programming Languages
items.summary: Although coding agents are now very effective in a variety of programming languages, this paper first shows that the cost (in tokens) can very significantly by programming language.
