Here, we investigate the theoretical and practical identifiability of a thinned Poisson point process model. We show that, with a log link for ecological intensity and a logit link for observation probability, the model can be structurally identifiable under simple conditions, provided that observation probability varies spatially. We then evaluate the benefits of using temporal replication within a spatio-temporal framework to improve estimation when ecological intensity and observation probability are weakly separated. We quantify these benefits through simulations. The results highlight persistent practical identifiability problems affecting the ecological and observation intercepts, especially when observation probabilities are low. However, in a spatio-temporal model with partial pooling, these parameters are estimated more accurately than in a single-year model, even when only a short time period is considered. Temporal replication also improves estimation of parameters shared across years. Finally, we illustrate the use of such a spatio-temporal model through a study of coypu (Myocastor coypus) distribution in Occitanie, France. Overall, our results show that temporal replication can partially alleviate practical identifiability problems in presence-only point process models when independent data sources are unavailable.

items.title: GaP-MoE : Explicit Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts via Orthogonal Gradient Accumulation and Projection
items.summary: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models improve scalability by routing input tokens to only a subset of expert networks, but they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity. Prior work has addressed this limitation either by improving router architectures or by introducing auxiliary loss terms that implicitly penalize similarity among experts. However, router-based approaches remain vulnerable to routing collapses, and loss-based approaches can conflict with the task's original objective during optimization. In this work, we propose GaP-MoE (Gradient Accumulation and Projection in MoE), which induces expert specialization by directly manipulating expert output gradients rather than modifying the loss function. At each training step, GaP-MoE stochastically selects one of the $TopK$ routed experts as a leader based on normalized routing scores, and projects the gradients of the remaining follower experts onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the leader's recent gradients. This removes directional overlap between expert gradients without altering the task loss, allowing specialization to emerge as a direct consequence of the optimization dynamics rather than an externally imposed constraint. We evaluate GaP-MoE in both fine-tuning settings (BERT-based, on GLUE) and from-scratch pretraining settings (GPT-2-based, on WikiText-103, enwik8, and text8), and further confirm its compatibility as a drop-in module for existing SMoE architectures. Experimental results show that GaP-MoE achieves performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.

items.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise
items.summary: Label noise presents a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning, especially when large-scale datasets are generated via automated processes. An increasingly common and important data paradigm, particularly in domains like medical imaging, involves learning from a large dataset with coarse, noisy labels supplemented by a small, expert-verified, clean dataset. This setting constitutes a typical information transfer and fusion problem. However, the significant distribution shift between the noisy and clean data violates the core overall parametric similarity assumptions of existing statistical transfer learning methods, while their reliance on parametric models is ill-suited for complex data like images. To address these limitations, this paper develops a generic model-agnostic nonparametric framework for classification with label noise, which applies to a broad class of classifiers. Our approach leverages the small clean dataset to ``purify'' the large noisy one and carefully manages the remaining ambiguous samples. This framework is underpinned by a rigorous statistical theory. Its empirical performance is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world application to medical image analysis for pneumonia diagnosis.

items.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
items.summary: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

items.title: Optimized Conformal Selection: Powerful Selective Inference After Data-Dependent Score Construction
items.summary: We study data-driven score construction in conformal selection, which uses conformal p-values and multiple testing to select "interesting" instances with large unobserved labels from a pool of unlabeled data, while controlling the FDR in finite sample. While existing solutions require the score function to be constructed independent of the calibration and test data, it is desirable to select or construct powerful conformity score in a data-driven manner and to leverage all labeled data for score training when presented with many score choices and limited labeled data. We propose Optimized Conformal Selection (OptCS), a general framework that allows valid multiple testing after flexible data-driven score construction. We introduce general conditions under which OptCS constructs valid conformal p-values despite substantial data reuse and handles complex p-value dependencies to maintain finite-sample FDR control. We instantiate this general recipe to propose three FDR-controlling procedures, each optimizing the models differently: (i) selecting a powerful score function among multiple candidates, (ii) training the score with all labeled data without sample splitting, and (iii) combining full-sample training and model selection. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methods via simulation studies and real applications in drug discovery and large language models.

items.title: Approximate Solomonoff Induction: On the Robustness of Learned Universal Predictors
items.summary: Why large language models trained via log-loss minimization over massive and diverse datasets exhibit broad capabilities and generalizable skills is not yet fully understood. Grau-Moya et al. (ICML 2024) offer a conceptual explanation through the lens of meta-learning: if sequence-generating environments $ν$ are drawn from a prior $w_ν$, minimizing population log-loss recovers the corresponding Bayesian mixture predictor $ξ=\sum_νw_νν$. In the idealized limit in which $w$ is a universal prior, the optimal predictor corresponds to Solomonoff universal induction. Practical machine learning algorithms, however, generally produce only \emph{approximately} optimal predictors. This raises a natural question: \emph{Does the prediction performance remain robust under approximation}? In this paper, we first provide a tight bound on the worst-case effect of approximation on prediction error. We show any predictor $ρ$ satisfying $D_{KL}(ξ\|ρ)\leq η$ retains bounded cumulative-expected-squared prediction error. However, while the Bayesian mixture predictor $ξ$ has error $O(\log(1/w_μ))$ in an environment $μ$, we establish a tight $Θ(η/w_μ)$ bound on the excess error of $ρ$ relative to $ξ$. Thus, approximation can substantially degrade performance in environments assigned small prior probability. In sharp contrast, when environments are averaged according to prior $w$, we prove that the excess prediction error is only $O(η)$. Furthermore, we establish a distribution-shift theorem for dominated shifts from a training prior $w$ to a test prior $w'$, interpolating our average-case and worst-case guarantees. Finally, we extend our robustness analysis to a finite-sampling setting relevant to learning universal predictors with neural networks and Transformers, where $D_{KL}(ξ\|ρ)$ could be unbounded. [For the full abstract, see the paper.]

items.title: Time-Uniform Dependent Central Limit Theory
items.summary: We establish a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure (FDM) framework. This result yields a universal time-uniform dependent central limit theorem, which serves as the basis for anytime-valid inference. In particular, we instantiate the theorem through asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs), time-uniform counterparts of asymptotic confidence intervals obtained via central limit theorems, extending those originally proposed in Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) to time series with serial dependence. We further refine their definition because, as we show, it can admit AsympCSs that fail to achieve the desired asymptotic time-uniform coverage for a broad class of data-generating processes, including independent and identically distributed cases. We address this issue by adding a simple eventual-inclusion condition, which in turn permits more flexible variance estimation, particularly useful in time-series settings. For feasible implementation of AsympCSs, we establish strong consistency of HAC variance estimators under the FDM framework, accommodating a wider range of commonly used bandwidth choices than existing results under mixing conditions. As illustrations, we construct AsympCSs for algorithms with Markovian structure and time-series-based causal estimands.

items.title: Uniformly Improved Adaptive Filtering Procedures for Replicability Testing with FWER Control
items.summary: Identifying signals that replicate across multiple studies is a fundamental challenge in modern data analysis. Partial conjunction (PC) testing addresses this problem by assessing whether a signal is present in at least a specified number of studies. The AdaFilter framework of Wang et al. (2022, Annals of Statistics 50, 1890-1909) improves the power of PC testing through adaptive filtering, but its family-wise error rate (FWER)-controlling procedures rely on conservative Bonferroni corrections at two stages: (i) the construction of PC $p$-values and filtering statistics, and (ii) the multiplicity adjustment used to control the FWER. We show that both stages can be improved using the Šidák correction. Under the same independence assumptions as the original AdaFilter framework, our improvements preserve finite-sample FWER control and guarantee at least as many rejections as their Bonferroni counterparts for every realisation of the data. Simulations and a real data analysis demonstrate the practical benefits of these improvements.

items.title: Generalised Robust Bayes for Joint Inference of Model and Contamination
items.summary: Robust generalised Bayesian methods protect parameter inference from contamination but do not generally infer its proportion or identify individual outliers. We propose Hölder--Bayes, which applies the Hölder divergence to a scaled model to construct a joint generalised posterior over model parameters and the contamination proportion, without specifying an outlier distribution. Each posterior draw flags a corresponding number of observations least compatible with the fitted model; averaging selections propagates joint uncertainty to outlier-detection scores. Under fixed, non-negligible contamination, we establish uniform boundedness of the posterior influence function, a finite-sample $n^{-1/2}$ bound on posterior-averaged excess risk, and a Bernstein--von Mises theorem. Tail overlap between the outlier distribution and the fitted model controls the population risk minimiser's bias and the associated change in limiting posterior covariance. Interpreting the posterior temperature as an affine volume scaling yields a closed-form, data-driven choice. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate robust estimation, contamination-proportion recovery, and posterior-guided data cleaning.

items.title: Schrödinger-Bass Bridge Barycenter Models for Measure-Valued Data
items.summary: Barycenter models, based on stochastic and deterministic optimal transport bridges between probability measures, have proven to be useful for supervised and unsupervised learning for (probability) measure-valued data. In this paper, we utilize the directional asymmetry and dual drift-diffusion control arising in the recently proposed Schrödinger-Bass Bridge (SBB) between two measures, and propose \textit{SBB-encoder}, \textit{SBB-decoder}, \textit{SBB-symmetric}, and \textit{SBB-Markovian} barycenter models. For each of these novel models, our first theoretical result establishes the existence of the SBB-barycenter under mild assumptions. Our second theoretical result characterizes the decoder SBB-barycenter of Gaussians where we show that for Gaussian input measures, the decoder formulation admits a Gaussian minimizer, reducing barycenter computation to a finite-dimensional optimization and yielding a compact algorithm. For general input measures, we derive a hybrid Wasserstein gradient particle descent scheme for all four formulations using the SBB dual representation. Finally, we utilize these algorithms for solving distributional-inverse/interpolation problems arising in the context of spatial images and single-cell RNA sequencing data, where we show that the SBB-decoder and Markovian barycenter allow us to interpolate between successive time points. Results show that our method outperforms existing barycenter models for measure interpolation and inference.

items.title: FRESH: Information-Geometric Calibration of Patient-Level Models to Aggregate Evidence
items.summary: This note introduces FRESH (Fusion of Recent Evidence and Subject Histories), a method for incorporating population-level summary results -- published clinical trials, registry summaries, prior natural-history studies, and peer-reviewed indirect comparisons -- into predictive models trained on patient-level data. This method provides a principled means of combining both patient-level and aggregate-level data types into a unified data-efficient model for clinical decision making. FRESH assumes access to a generative model trained on patient-level data sources (e.g. clinical trial or real-world data). The method produces patient-level predictions from a re-calibrated model that matches a set of specified aggregate statistics for a target population. This can be understood as a patient-level recapitulation of the aggregate source -- with the key property that the recalibration is a minimal perturbation of the original joint distribution in a specific information-geometric sense. The resulting samples can be analyzed directly or combined into a post-training procedure to update the original generative model. This approach enables several applications where rigorously incorporating patient-level data with summary information is valuable, including (i) contextualizing single-arm trial results with respect to recent standard-of-care, (ii) clinical-trial simulations for design and probability-of-technical-success estimation, and (iii) comparative-effectiveness analyses of on-market therapies.

items.title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
items.summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.

items.title: Asymptotically Exact Negative Guidance of Diffusion Models via Positive-Unlabeled Learning
items.summary: Negative guidance of diffusion models generates samples that avoid an undesired condition, specified either by reference samples or by a conditional score alongside an unconditional model. Existing methods inject repulsive terms derived from local information at each sample, so the resulting sampler does not target an explicit density, and its bias cannot be systematically reduced by increasing computation. We instead present a negative-guidance method that samples from an explicit target density, which uniformly handles both reference-sample and score-based specifications and suppresses probability mass near the undesired condition with an avoidance strength that parametrizes the target density itself. Realizing this target requires estimating, at each diffusion timestep, how likely each sample is to belong to the undesired condition. We cast this estimation as a Positive-Unlabeled learning problem that admits lightweight online training along the diffusion trajectory, using condition samples as positives and diffusion particles as unlabeled data. Because the guided particles drift from the unconditional marginal, we further correct the residual mismatch via Sequential Monte Carlo, yielding a sampler that is asymptotically exact in the particle limit and that turns any existing negative-guidance method into its proposal kernel. Empirically, our method approaches the ground-truth target on Gaussian mixtures and Pareto-dominates existing methods on trade-offs between avoidance and generation quality, distributional bias, and diversity, including in an image-generation setting with a pretrained score network.

items.title: Data-Adaptive Multi-Bin Rarefying for Alpha Diversity Association Analysis under Heterogeneous Library Sizes
items.summary: Alpha diversity association analysis is sensitive to heterogeneous library sizes, and overall rarefying to a common depth can either discard many reads from high-depth samples or exclude low-depth samples. We propose MBRarefy, a data-adaptive framework for selecting multi-bin rarefying designs. The method chooses library size cutpoints by minimizing an objective that combines residual within-bin library size dependence with a fragmentation penalty, subject to a minimum bin size constraint. The framework supports both fixed-K and varying-K cutpoint selection. In T-cell receptor (TCR) motivated simulations, the primary fixed-K procedure controlled depth-induced false positives and improved power relative to overall rarefying when group and depth confounding was absent. Applications to TCR immunosequencing and wild baboon gut microbiome data illustrate its ability to reduce residual library size dependence while improving read and sample retention.

items.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
items.summary: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.

items.title: Memorizing Long-tail Data Can Help Generalization Through Composition
items.summary: Deep learning has led researchers to rethink the relationship between memorization and generalization. In many settings, memorization does not hurt generalization due to implicit regularization and may help by memorizing long-tailed examples. In this paper, we consider the synergy between memorization and simple composition -- the ability to make correct prediction on a combination of long-tailed features. Theoretically, we show that for a linear setting, memorization together with composition can help the model make correct predictions on rare test examples that require a combination of long-tailed features, even if such combinations were never observed in the training data. Experiments on neural network architecture on simple data show that the theoretical insight extends beyond the linear setting, and we further observe that the composition capability of the model depends on its architecture.

items.title: Adaptive auditing of AI systems with anytime-valid guarantees
items.summary: A major bottleneck in characterizing the failure modes of generative AI systems is the cost and time of annotation and evaluation. Consequently, adaptive testing paradigms have gained popularity, where one opportunistically decides which cases and how many to annotate based on past results. While this framework is highly practical, its extreme flexibility makes it difficult to draw statistically rigorous conclusions, as it violates classical assumptions: the number of observations is typically limited (often 10 to 50 cases) and decisions regarding sampling and stopping are made in the midst of data collection rather than based a pre-specified rule. To characterize what statistical inferences can be drawn from highly adaptive audits, we introduce a hypothesis testing framework from two "dueling" perspectives: (i) the model's null that asserts there is no failure mode with performance below a target threshold versus (ii) the auditor's null that asserts they have a sampling strategy that will uncover a failure mode. Leveraging Safe Anytime-Valid Inference (SAVI), we formalize the auditor as conducting "testing by betting," which translates into simultaneous e-processes for testing the dueling null hypotheses. Furthermore, if the auditor is sufficiently powerful, we prove that these two hypotheses are asymptotically inverses of each other, in that passage of such an audit certifies the AI system as being globally robust. Empirically, we demonstrate that our proposed testing procedures maintain anytime-valid Type-I error control, outperform pre-specified testing methods, and can reach statistically rigorous conclusions sometimes with as few as 20 observations.

items.title: Online Augmented Plug-in Inference for Multi-group Fair Prediction
items.summary: Fairness regularization changes both a prediction rule and its sampling uncertainty. We develop online inference for classifiers trained with a covariance penalty on group mean decision scores, a tractable proxy for demographic parity. The framework includes logistic regression and smoothed support-vector machines, with linear regression as a special case targeting equality of group mean predictions. The inferential challenge arises because the fairness operator is estimated from the same stream used to update the predictor. Each observation contributes to its current loss gradient and to subsequent penalty estimates, creating an additional first-order fluctuation in the Polyak--Ruppert average. We derive an asymptotic expansion with harmonic reuse weights and an augmented covariance incorporating score variation, operator variation, and their dependence. Exact fixed-memory recursions yield a consistent covariance estimator and asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the penalized coefficients. Simulation studies assess coverage and interval contraction. Adult-income classification and IPUMS wage regression illustrate coefficient uncertainty and fairness--utility trade-offs, with classification demographic parity evaluated separately through threshold decisions.

items.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
items.summary: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.

items.title: Rare-Feature-Adaptive Subsampling for Big Data Regression
items.summary: Rare binary features cause instability and slow convergence in regression. Subsampling massive datasets may discard observations carrying rare-feature information. We show that rare-feature coefficient convergence rates depend on feature prevalence and the inclusion probabilities assigned to rare observations. This finding motivates subsampling designs that adapt sampling probabilities to feature rarity. We first study optimal rare-census designs, which extend the negative subsampling approach by retaining every rare observation. However, they may face practical constraints. We then propose a computationally efficient rarity-adaptive L-optimal design that incorporates inverse prevalence scaling. Because implementing optimal designs requires pilot estimates whose quality depends on adequate representation of rare features, we propose a balanced design, a one-step rarity-adaptive design based only on binary features. It can be used alone, as a pilot, or combined with designs targeting other objectives. For implementation in two stages, we develop a union-sample estimator that reuses pilot observations while accounting for sample overlap and establish its asymptotic normality. Simulations and applications show improved stability and estimation efficiency over existing methods. One application evaluates designs that jointly protect rare outcomes and rare features.

items.title: Structured Temporal Causality for Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
items.summary: Real-world multivariate time series anomalies are rare and often unlabeled. Additionally, prevailing methods rely on increasingly complex architectures tuned to benchmarks, detecting only fragments of anomalous segments and overstating performance. In this paper, we introduce OracleAD, a simple and interpretable unsupervised framework for multivariate time series anomaly detection. OracleAD encodes each variable's past sequence into a single causal embedding to jointly predict the present time point and reconstruct the input window, effectively modeling temporal dynamics. These embeddings then undergo a self-attention mechanism to project them into a shared latent space and capture spatial relationships. These relationships are not static, since they are modeled by a property that emerges from each variable's temporal dynamics. The projected embeddings are aligned to a Stable Latent Structure (SLS) representing normal-state relationships. Anomalies are identified using a dual scoring mechanism based on prediction error and deviation from the SLS, enabling fine-grained anomaly diagnosis at each time point and across individual variables. Since any noticeable SLS deviation originates from embeddings that violate the learned temporal causality of normal data, OracleAD directly pinpoints the root-cause variables at the embedding level. OracleAD achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple real-world datasets and evaluation protocols, while remaining interpretable through SLS.

items.title: Network Cross-Validation and Model Selection via Subsampling
items.summary: Complex and larger networks are becoming increasingly prevalent in scientific applications in various domains. Although a number of models and methods exist for such networks, cross-validation on networks remains challenging due to the unique structure of network data. In this paper, we propose a general cross-validation procedure called NETCROP (NETwork CRoss-Validation using Overlapping Partitions). The key idea is to divide the original network into multiple subnetworks with a shared overlap part, producing training sets consisting of the subnetworks and a test set with the node pairs between the subnetworks. This train-test split provides the basis for a network cross-validation procedure that can be applied on a wide range of model selection and parameter tuning problems for networks. The method is computationally efficient for large networks as it uses smaller subnetworks for the training step. We provide methodological details and theoretical guarantees for several model selection and parameter tuning tasks using NETCROP. Numerical results demonstrate that NETCROP performs accurate cross-validation on a diverse set of network model selection and parameter tuning problems. The results also indicate that NETCROP is computationally much faster while being often more accurate than the existing methods for network cross-validation.

items.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series
items.summary: Identifying relationships among stochastic processes is a core objective in many fields, such as economics. While the standard toolkit for multivariate time series analysis has many advantages, it can be difficult to capture nonlinear dynamics using linear vector autoregressive models. This difficulty has motivated the development of methods for causal discovery and variable selection for nonlinear time series, which routinely employ tests for conditional independence. In this paper, we introduce the first framework for conditional independence testing that works with a single realization of a nonstationary nonlinear process. The proposed test is designed to have power against alternatives in which the expected conditional covariance is non-zero for at least some times. We also discuss an approach for gaining power against a broader range of alternatives. The key technical ingredients of our framework are time-varying nonlinear regression, estimation of local long-run covariance matrices of products of error processes, and a distribution-uniform strong Gaussian approximation.

items.title: Forge: An Agentic System for ERGM Specification and Interpretation in Social Networks
items.summary: Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) provide a statistical framework for testing hypotheses about how ties form using network structure and node attributes. Their usefulness depends on model specification, which often requires researchers to repeatedly propose models, fit them, check how well they reproduce the observed network, and revise them when they do not. We present Forge (Formation-Oriented Reasoning with Guarded ERGMs), an agentic system that performs this process using a language model and external statistical tools. Given an observed network and a domain description, Forge proposes hypotheses about tie formation, translates them into candidate ERGM specifications, evaluates them statistically, refines the best candidate using goodness-of-fit feedback, and returns a human-readable interpretation of the final model. On 16 benchmark networks, Forge improves on the best baseline on 13 networks and matches it on the other three, with a median 24.8% improvement in goodness of fit. On 60 controlled networks with known generating specifications, Forge achieves exact specification recovery in 78.3% of cases and attains 90.8% term-level F1. These results show that Forge can reduce the manual trial-and-error involved in ERGM specification while making the process more reproducible and keeping model selection grounded in statistical evidence.

items.title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
items.summary: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.

items.title: Generalized survival energy models with exogenous covariates for mortality prediction
items.summary: We develop a generalized survival energy model that relates mortality to social and economic conditions through a latent energy process. Death occurs when this process first reaches or crosses zero. Environmental covariates enter the coefficients governing depletion, recovery, fluctuations and accumulated damage, yielding lifetime distributions conditional on the environmental path. We derive these distributions for diffusion and inverse Gaussian specifications and describe their numerical evaluation. An application to Japanese male and female mortality data assesses predictive performance against Cairns--Blake--Dowd benchmarks. Conditional on realized environmental paths, the selected inverse Gaussian models achieve small prediction errors comparable to those of the benchmarks. The framework also provides a model-based interpretation of how environmental changes affect mortality through the rate of damage accumulation or the magnitude of energy fluctuations. These interpretations describe conditional statistical relationships rather than causal effects. The resulting models offer a way to study mortality under alternative environmental scenarios while retaining a connection to classical actuarial survival models.

items.title: Estimand frameworks for causal inference in clinical research and regulatory decision making
items.summary: Causal inference for clinical and regulatory decision making requires a precise definition of the causal estimand, that is, what we want to estimate. Three frameworks are commonly used to describe causal estimands: PICO and its extensions, the target trial framework, and the E9(R1) Addendum of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH). Because these frameworks were developed by different scientific communities, they operate at different levels of detail, emphasize different aspects of the causal estimand, and use different terminology for closely related concepts. Here we compare the three frameworks and translate across their terminologies. PICO is a compact framework that helps jumpstart a conversation about the causal question, but it does not encode sufficient information to fully characterize a causal estimand. The target trial framework characterizes the causal estimand precisely by specifying the components of the protocol of the randomized trial that would answer the causal question: eligibility criteria, treatment strategies, assignment, outcome, start and end of follow-up, and causal contrast. E9(R1) starts from intercurrent events and lists strategies to address them, some of which describe estimators rather than estimands, or imply estimands that are not relevant to decision makers or cannot be estimated under reasonable assumptions. We argue that the target trial framework subsumes the other two, and we provide a map of the correspondences across the three frameworks.

items.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Conjoint Experiments
items.summary: Choosing an appropriate sample size is a fundamental challenge in experimental design. This challenge is particularly salient in conjoint experiments, where researchers simultaneously target many estimands whose inferential goals may be reached at different sample sizes. Conventional sample-size calculations address this challenge in an ex ante manner. In large online studies, including many conjoint experiments, data often arrive continuously, allowing researchers to dynamically stop data collection. In such settings, the relevant practical question is not "what sample size should I choose in advance?" but rather, as data accumulate, "have I learned enough yet?" A naive response is to repeatedly inspect conventional confidence intervals and $p$-values, but doing so invalidates their inferential guarantees. We address this challenge by developing a general anytime-valid framework for conjoint experiments that allows continuous monitoring and data-dependent stopping. This framework equips many common conjoint estimands with asymptotic $e$-processes, confidence sequences, and anytime-valid $p$-values, and provides a general recipe for any estimand that can be expressed as a linear contrast of population OLS coefficients. Across common conjoint settings, we demonstrate that anytime-valid inference can yield substantial sample savings relative to fixed-sample designs. The probability of early stopping frequently exceeds 50%, with mean sample savings often surpassing 25%.

items.title: From Common Information to Canonical Correlation Analysis and Beyond: Bridging Information Theory, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning
items.summary: Many problems in signal processing, machine learning, and neuroimaging provide several jointly observed measurements of one process, each mixing a component common to all of them with a component private to itself, and require the common component to be recovered without supervision. This problem has been studied in several communities, largely independently. Statisticians proposed canonical correlation analysis (CCA), introduced by Hotelling in 1936. Information theorists proposed two notions of common information, due to Gács and Körner and to Wyner. Engineers developed subspace methods for sensor arrays and multiuser communications to design multiview receivers. This tutorial presents the main results and tools each community developed for this problem in a single exposition, and explains the connections that emerge where they meet, distinguishing exact equivalences from special cases and analogies. We develop the information-theoretic foundation from first principles. We then introduce CCA and its extension to several views, followed by the engineering thread from blind multiuser detection to CCA as a blind receiver. Next, we turn to nonlinear CCA, covering kernel, deep, and probabilistic formulations, the conditions under which the common factor is identifiable, and connections to self-supervised learning. We conclude with a discussion of further extensions and open directions. The exposition is self-contained, so that readers from each of these communities can follow the parts developed by the others.

items.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study
items.summary: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: \textit{is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice?} To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: \textit{sufficient-statistic invariance} and the \textit{martingale property}. We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.

items.title: A LATE-Targeting Experimental Design for Multi-Arm RCTs
items.summary: We study the design of multi-arm experiments that identify local average treatment effects under imperfect compliance. With three or more arms, conventional randomization fails to identify margin-specific effects even under strong extensions of monotone compliance. A choice-theoretic analysis unifies these extensions and motivates a two-stage design: subjects report a preferred arm and are randomized conditional on it. If treatment is confined to the assigned or reported arm, one-sided noncompliance is restored conditional on the report, identifying the effect between the two for their compliers. We discuss the design's applicability and feasibility in relation to the choice model.

items.title: A note on conditional densities, Bayes' rule, and recent criticisms of Bayesian inference
items.summary: When performing Bayesian inference, we frequently need to work with conditional probability densities. For example, the posterior function is the conditional density of the parameters given the data. Some might worry that conditional densities are ill-defined, considering that for a continuous random variable $Y$, the event $\{Y=y\}$ has probability zero, meaning the formula $\mathbb{P}(A|B)=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(B)$ is inapplicable. In reality, when we work with conditional densities, we never condition directly on the zero-probability event $\{Y=y\}$; rather, we first condition on the random variable $Y$, and then we may plug in an observed value $y$. The first purpose of our article is to provide an exposition on conditional densities that elaborates on this point. While we have aimed to make this explanation accessible, we follow it with a roadmap of the measure theory needed to make it rigorous. A recent preprint (arXiv:2411.13570) has expressed the concern that probability densities are ill-defined and that as a result Bayes' theorem cannot be used, and they provide examples that allegedly demonstrate inconsistencies in the Bayesian framework. The second purpose of our article is to investigate their claims. We contend that the examples given in their work do not demonstrate any inconsistencies; we find that there are mathematical errors and that they deviate significantly from the Bayesian framework.

items.title: Detecting Model Misspecification in Bayesian Inverse Problems via Variational Gradient Descent
items.summary: Bayesian inference is optimal when the statistical model is well-specified, while outside this setting Bayesian inference can catastrophically fail; accordingly a wealth of post-Bayesian methodologies have been proposed. Predictively oriented (PrO) approaches lift the statistical model $P_θ$ to an (infinite) mixture model $\int P_θ\; \mathrm{d}Q(θ)$ and fit this predictive distribution via minimising an entropy-regularised objective functional. In the well-specified setting one expects the mixing distribution $Q$ to concentrate around the true data-generating parameter in the large data limit, while such singular concentration will typically not be observed if the model is misspecified. Our contribution is to demonstrate that one can empirically detect model misspecification by comparing the standard Bayesian posterior to the PrO `posterior' $Q$, providing a novel and widely-applicable diagnostic tool for the standard Bayesian workflow. To operationalise this, we present an efficient numerical algorithm based on variational gradient descent. A simulation study, and a more detailed case study involving a Bayesian inverse problem in seismology, confirm that model misspecification can be automatically detected using this framework.

items.title: Bayesian Semiparametric Multivariate Density Regression with Coordinate-Wise Predictor Selection
items.summary: We propose a flexible Bayesian approach for estimating the joint density of a multivariate random variable of interest in the presence of categorical covariates. Leveraging a Gaussian copula framework, our method captures the dependence structure across different coordinates of the multivariate response. The conditional (on covariates) marginal (across outcomes) distributions are modeled as flexible mixtures with shared atoms across coordinates. The mixture weights are allowed to vary with covariates through a novel Tucker tensor factorization-based structure which enables the identification of coordinate-specific subsets of influential covariates. In particular, we replace the traditional mode matrices with coordinate-specific random partition models on the covariate levels, offering a flexible mechanism to aggregate covariate levels that exhibit similar effects on the response. We introduce a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that scales with the number of aggregated levels rather than the original levels, significantly reducing memory requirements and improving computational efficiency. We demonstrate the method's numerical performance through simulation experiments and its practical applicability through the analysis of NHANES dietary data.

items.title: Covariate-assisted graph matching
items.summary: Data integration often requires aligning datasets without unique identifiers; for network data this is commonly addressed through graph matching. Despite the widespread availability of node and edge covariates in many applications, most existing methods rely solely on the structural similarity between the two graphs, limiting their flexibility and robustness to non-identifiable matches and structural noise. In this article, we study the seeded graph matching problem, where a partial alignment for a set of nodes (seeds) is known, in the presence of informative node and edge covariates. We propose two covariate-assisted methods: a global approach based on a quadratic assignment problem (QAP), and a scalable local approach that leverages the neighborhood of the seeds. Both methods are based on a flexible conditional modeling framework that enables covariate integration using predictive models ranging from generalized linear models to machine learning methods. We provide estimation error rates for the generalized linear model, and sufficient conditions for exact recovery of the true correspondences via the QAP. We further specialize these results to Erdős-Rényi model with covariates. The effectiveness in achieving improved performance by leveraging additional covariates is demonstrated through simulations and in an application to matching the statistics academic genealogy and the collaboration networks.

items.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
items.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.

items.title: A Computable Measure of Suboptimality for Entropy-Regularised Variational Objectives
items.summary: Several methods in statistics and machine learning target a probability distribution for which an entropy-regularised variational objective is minimised. This increased flexibility introduces a computational challenge, as one loses access to an explicit unnormalised density for the target. To mitigate this difficulty, we introduce a novel measure of suboptimality called 'gradient discrepancy', and in particular a kernel gradient discrepancy (KGD) that can be explicitly computed. In the Bayesian statistics context, KGD coincides with the kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD), and we obtain a novel characterisation of KSD as measuring the size of a variational gradient. Outside this familiar setting, KGD enables novel sampling algorithms to be developed and compared, even when unnormalised densities cannot be obtained. To illustrate this point several novel algorithms are proposed and studied, including a natural generalisation of Stein variational gradient descent, with applications to mean-field neural networks and predictively oriented posteriors presented. On the theoretical side, our principal contribution is to establish sufficient conditions for desirable properties of KGD, such as continuity and convergence control.

items.title: Dual-Phase Flow Matching for Probabilistic Source Detection and Measurement in Astronomical Images
items.summary: Using the largest digital camera ever built, the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will image over half the night sky. Most astronomical analyses of LSST data operate not on images but on catalogs derived from them: tables of light sources detailing their positions, fluxes (colors and brightnesses), and types (e.g., star, galaxy). At LSST's imaging depths, light sources often overlap visually, so the configuration of sources in each image is itself uncertain. Nevertheless, LSST's cataloging pipeline commits to a single source configuration, which can bias downstream analyses. Here, we instead approximate a posterior distribution over source configurations. Our posterior approximation is a continuous-time Markov process (CTMP) fitted by generator matching, an extension of flow matching to non-Euclidean state spaces. This CTMP generates a source configuration in two phases: it detects light sources in the first and measures them in the second. On simulated LSST-like data, the proposed method produces better posterior approximations than five comparison methods: two Markov chain Monte Carlo methods that run thousands of times more slowly at survey scales; two neural posterior estimation methods; and one ablation of the proposed method that lacks the dual-phase structure. Applied to LSST Data Preview 1 (DP1), the first public release of Rubin imaging, the proposed method alone recovers small-scale galaxy clustering in agreement with higher-resolution Hubble imaging and reports uncertainty that remains calibrated against that reference as blending increases. We deliver a probabilistic catalog of the Extended Chandra Deep Field South region, one of the most extensively studied extragalactic fields, and use it to characterize the galaxy color-magnitude distribution.

items.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
items.summary: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

items.title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series
items.summary: Inference for time series of networks often relies on accurate vertex correspondence between network realizations at different times. In practice, such vertex alignments can be misspecified or unknown. We study the impact of errorful vertex alignment on changepoint localization for dynamic networks through two illustrative models, with the key distinction being whether changepoint information is contained in marginal or joint distributions of the time-varying latent positions. We compare localization techniques ranging from the simple network statistic of average degree to the modern procedure of Euclidean mirrors. Our results demonstrate that understanding the interplay of marginal and joint information in the observed network time series is key to robust network inference.

items.title: Actually, All Learnable Distribution Classes Are Privately Learnable
items.summary: We show that every class of distributions that is learnable up to arbitrarily small target error in total variation distance with finitely many samples is also learnable under ($\varepsilon, δ$)-differential privacy up to arbitrarily small target error with finitely many samples. This proves a conjecture of Ashtiani. Previous work by Bun, Kamath, Mouzakis, and Singhal [arXiv:2402.00267] gave a weak refutation of this conjecture, showing that this implication is not true when learnability is defined with respect to a fixed target error. In contrast, we show that, under the standard definition of learnability, the conjecture is true.

items.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?
items.summary: In recent years it has been claimed that new political parties are shut out of the UK House of Commons because they are rarely elected. At the same time, general political understanding seems to be that the House of Commons is currently further away from a pure two-party distribution of seats than at any time in the past century, perhaps longer. Although this might seem like a paradox it is possible for both of these things to have credence. We present an analysis that shows that the number of new political parties elected to the House of Commons has been slowly declining over the last century. We illustrate this both by regression and Good-Turing analyses. We also analyse the lifetime and persistence of political parties as well as present metrics that indicate the recent increased political diversity and identify the nadir of diversity in the mid-1960s and early 1970s.

items.title: Calibration scoring under dependent seed variables in Cooke's Classical Model: a Mehler-Hermite design-effect correction
items.summary: Cooke's Classical Model scores the statistical accuracy of experts by the $p$-value of a likelihood ratio test that compares the bin frequencies of realized seed variables with nominal probabilities, using a $χ^2$ reference. This calibration score drives performance-based weights and implicitly assumes independent seed variables, although seeds often share a common driver, such as the same indicator in several regions or periods. Under dependence the statistic converges to a weighted sum of $χ^2_1$ variables, and positive dependence makes the classical score anti-conservative. Under a Gaussian-copula working model, a Mehler-Hermite expansion gives the long-run covariance of the bin indicators in closed form, defines a design effect and an effective number of seed variables, and shows that the first-order correction coincides with the ad hoc calibration power of existing software. Rao-Scott-type and parametric-bootstrap corrected scores are proposed, together with a restricted maximum likelihood estimator of the nuisance dependence, computed from rank normal scores and invariant to location-scale miscalibration, and a prepivoted bootstrap that propagates its uncertainty. In simulations the classical score rejects up to 68\% of calibrated experts at a nominal 5\% level, whereas the corrected scores remove most of the excess rejection. In 45 published studies, design effects of 1.25-2 shift more than 5\% of the optimized weight in 29-44\% of studies. In three social-science studies with structured seeds, the baseline estimates imply that 18-21 seed variables carry the information of only 11-13 independent ones, although conclusions about individual experts depend on how the dependence is specified.

items.title: Depth Separation for Neural Networks under Gaussian Measure
items.summary: We revisit the problem of depth separation for neural networks, as studied by Eldan and Shamir, Daniely, and others. Specifically, we consider the natural setting of $L^2$ approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in $d$ dimensions. We show that there is a radial function in $L^2$ under the standard Gaussian measure that can be approximated to a fixed sufficiently small $L^2$ error by a depth-3 ReLU neural network of polynomial size in $d$ but can only be approximated by depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights if their size is at least exponential in $d$. For that, we prove a general result showing that if a radial function has substantial mass in the high frequencies of its Hermite expansion, then it cannot be well approximated by a depth-2 neural network with small width and bounded weights. All theorems, lemmas, propositions, and corollaries are verified in Lean~4.

items.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
items.summary: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

items.title: Sharp spectral norm concentration and regularization of sparse random tensors
items.summary: We prove sharp spectral-norm bounds and construct a mean-fitting regularization procedure for sparse random tensors of fixed order $k$. For an $n\times\cdots\times n$ tensor with independentBernoulli$(p)$ entries, the centered norm is $O(\sqrt{np})$ with polynomially high probability whenever $np\ge c\log n$. This removes the logarithmic loss in Zhou and Zhu (2021). We also determine the expected centered norm at every sparsity level: for every $0<p\le1/2$, it has order $\min\{n^kp,\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{eff}}}\}$, where $d_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is an effective degree accounting for unusually large fiber counts. The upper bounds extend to tensors with deterministic entrywise weights and unequal sampling probabilities. Analogous two-sided bounds hold for the Friedman--Wigderson model at every degree; its expected centered norm has order $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{eff}}}$. We also give an all-sparsity regularization procedure for independent Bernoulli tensors with unknown, possibly unequal means in $[0,p]$. Our light-fitting regularization estimates the original mean with minimax expected spectral-norm error of order $\min\{\sqrt{np},pn^{k/2}\}$ for every known $0\le p\le1$. The procedure fits light multilinear residuals under an entrywise constraint on the candidate mean, rather than deleting high-degree fibers.

items.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamical Clustering of Time Series
items.summary: We present a method that models the evolution of an unbounded number of time series clusters by switching among an unknown number of regimes with linear dynamics. We develop a Bayesian non-parametric approach using a hierarchical Dirichlet process as a prior on the parameters of a Switching Linear Dynamical System and a Gaussian process prior to model the statistical variations in amplitude and temporal alignment within each cluster. By modeling the evolution of time series patterns, the method avoids unnecessary proliferation of clusters in a principled manner. We perform inference by formulating a variational lower bound for off-line and on-line scenarios, enabling efficient learning through optimization. We illustrate the versatility and effectiveness of the approach through several case studies of electrocardiogram analysis using publicly available databases.

items.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
items.summary: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

items.title: A general class of shared gamma frailty models for risk prediction, with application to breast cancer screening adherence
items.summary: We introduce a new class of mixed models for longitudinal or clustered binary data. The formulation is inspired by the shared frailty multivariate survival model for clustered data, and it allows for closed forms for all the relevant quantities, which allows for an efficient and fast computational solution of the associated inferential and prediction problems. We focus on an easily interpretable specification of the model, discuss the associated individual risk prediction, and compare our results to the traditional GLMM model for binary data with random intercept. We implement the methods on a large motivating dataset on the individual longitudinal adherence to the breast cancer screening program of the Oslo region.

items.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
items.summary: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.

items.title: Multi-Marginal Inverse Optimal Transport for Contrastive Learning Via Explicit Anchor-Positive-Negative Coupling
items.summary: Inverse Optimal Transport (OT) based methods for representation learning learn representations such that the global OT coupling between a pair of data marginals in the representation space, concentrates on the positive pairs. This is in contrast to previous methods that primarily focused on pairwise matching. However, these methods $\textit{DO NOT}$ utilize negative pairs and hence are not truly contrastive in their approach. We show that this leads to issues of dimensional collapse and hence degraded downstream performance. To alleviate this, we develop a novel multi-marginal (MM) inverse OT (IOT) contrastive learning (CL) approach called Neg-MMIOT-CL, which learns representations such that the global multi-marginal OT (MMOT) coupling between a triple of data marginals, with respect to a carefully designed ground-cost between triplets of data points in the representation space, concentrates on the anchor-positive-negative $\textit{triplets}$. For a latent class model, we empirically show that Neg-MMIOT-CL alleviates dimensional collapse. Furthermore, for a specific choice of ground cost for all triplets in representation space, we prove that the optimal representation configuration for Neg-MMIOT-CL exhibits equiangular property for within-class and across-class representations, which translates to Neural-Collapse when the representation dimension is larger than the number of classes minus one -- a result that is $\textit{previously established only}$ for pairwise contrastive learning methods. Finally, we propose Neg-IOT-CL-PushPull, that is a computationally efficient alternative to Neg-MMIOT-CL, alleviating the high cost of computing MMOT plans needed during implementation. We apply these methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets and show significant improvements over existing OT-based contrastive learning methods.

items.title: Estimation and Inference for Causal Explainability
items.summary: Understanding how much each variable contributes to an outcome is a central question across disciplines. A causal view of explainability is favorable for its ability in uncovering underlying mechanisms and generalizing to new contexts. Based on a family of causal explainability quantities, we develop methods for their estimation and inference. In particular, we construct a one-step correction estimator using semi-parametric efficiency theory, which explicitly leverages the independence structure of variables to reduce the asymptotic variance. For a null hypothesis on the boundary, i.e., zero explainability, we show its equivalence to Fisher's sharp null, which motivates a randomization-based inference procedure. Finally, we illustrate the empirical efficacy of our approach through simulations as well as an immigration experiment dataset, where we investigate how features and their interactions shape public opinion toward admitting immigrants.

items.title: Borrowing Strength Across Stores: Transfer Learning for Choice-Based Revenue Management
items.summary: Large retail chains must tailor assortment and pricing decisions to local customer preferences, yet even retailers with extensive sales records often have limited data for estimating demand at the store or local market level, particularly in product categories with short selling windows. Local estimation (fitting a demand model for each store on its own) can therefore be unreliable, while pooling data across stores improves estimation precision at the cost of ignoring local demand heterogeneity. We study how retailers can balance these competing effects through transfer learning under a multinomial logit (MNL) demand model. We propose a shrinkage estimator that combines store-specific demand estimates with information pooled from other stores. Unlike the linear or quadratic settings underlying much of the existing theoretical literature on information transfer in operations, the nonlinear MNL likelihood does not admit a straightforward bias-variance decomposition. By exploiting its self-concordant-like properties, we establish finite-sample performance guarantees that characterize when information transfer improves demand estimation and how the appropriate degree of shrinkage depends on local sample size, feature dimensionality, and cross-store heterogeneity. We further derive regret bounds for downstream assortment and pricing decisions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the operational benefits of shrinkage across different data environments. An empirical study using data from several hundred stores of a European apparel retailer shows that shrinkage improves out-of-sample product prioritization and revenue capture relative to both local estimation and full pooling. Our findings demonstrate how retailers can leverage information across their store networks to improve revenue management decisions while preserving local demand differences.

items.title: The Trilemma of Truth in Large Language Models
items.summary: The public often attributes human-like qualities to large language models (LLMs), assuming that they "know" certain things. In reality, LLMs encode information retained during training as internal probabilistic knowledge. This study examines existing methods for probing the veracity of that knowledge and identifies three flawed underlying assumptions. To address these flaws, we introduce sAwMIL (Sparse-Aware Multiple-Instance Learning), a multiclass probing framework that combines multiple-instance learning with conformal prediction. sAwMIL leverages LLMs' internal representations to classify statements as true, false, or neither. We evaluate sAwMIL across 16 open-source LLMs, including default and chat-based variants, using three new curated datasets. Our results show that (1) common probing methods fail to provide a reliable and transferable veracity direction and, in some settings, perform worse than zero-shot prompting; (2) truth and falsehood are not encoded symmetrically; and (3) LLMs encode a third type of signal that is distinct from both true and false.

items.title: Do Neural Models Prefer Their Submodels?
items.summary: A neural model is the set of functions that can be expressed by a given neural network architecture. Neural models contain natural submodels, such as those obtained by setting some neurons to be inactive. We study the geometry of neural models and ask whether they prefer their submodels. By this we mean whether local minimizers of the loss function lie in a given submodel. We introduce a geometric framework to determine if this occurs. For shallow multilayer perceptrons, we show that subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are never preferred. For deep multilayer perceptrons, we give conditions under which subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are not preferred. For lightning self-attention, lower-rank submodels are usually not preferred, but we identify examples where they are because they lie on a boundary of the model. Our results show that, aside from a few exceptions, preference for submodels cannot be explained by the geometry of the neural model, and must instead come from other sources such as training dynamics.

items.title: Exact Covariance Structure and Efficient Computation for L-Comoments
items.summary: L-moments are useful summary statistics and so have been widely employed in statistical analysis. L-comoments provide a multivariate generalization of L-moments. Joint finite-sample covariance structure, which represents the sampling uncertainty, of L-comoments is less well understood than that of univariate L-moments. We thus derive exact finite-sample covariance formulas for sample L-comoments using explicit conditional U-statistic kernels. We further construct an asymptotic projection estimator and an unbiased estimator of the finite-sample covariance matrix and develop positive-definite corrections. An efficient rank-prefix algorithm evaluates the full unbiased covariance estimator in $O(n^2)$ time without enumerating disjoint subsets. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial computational savings. The results provide a basis for first-order covariance approximations for L-comoment ratios and for subsequent multivariate L-moment estimation.

items.title: Interpretable subgroup identification across survival and generalized-linear outcomes
items.summary: A subgroup analysis searching a trial's covariates or many prespecified subgroups often singles out a subgroup for its extremity, interpreted as if prespecified. Selection inflates the estimate; for a given selection rule, a correction removes the inflation. Two questions belong to the rule: which candidate to return, and whether to declare none. A third is whether inference extends to the patients left outside. We treat all three for interpretable subgroups, defined by conjunctions of covariate cuts, generated by forest search, a causal forest or a cross-fit surface estimator under one set of rules, each a modelling choice trading size against effect. Forest search screens candidates on splitting consistency, the rate at which effects replicate across half-splits; the screen is complementary-pairs stability selection in closed form, and the law of the maximum over the family gives the family-wise false-declaration rate when every candidate's effect is at least a clinically specified benefit. Refit-free multiplier resampling gives adjusted one-sided bounds (subgroup and complement), joined in a two-subgroup claim, with coverage asymptotically exact under separated selection, characterized under local competition, and conditional on a family proposed from the outcomes. Two trial applications, and simulations built from them, cover survival, binary and continuous endpoints.

items.title: Confessions of a Masked MDP
