In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.

items.title: Robust Capital Budgeting
items.summary: We study capital budgeting when a manager privately knows project productivity and her empire-building benefits, while headquarters lacks credible priors. Headquarters minimizes maximum regret relative to informed investment. Without compensation, the optimal policy is a spending cap balancing empire-building overinvestment against profitable investment forgone. Compensation helps when empire-building incentives are weak. The optimal payment incentivizes restraint, declines with investment, and reaches zero at the spending cap, supporting greater managerial discretion. When empire-building incentives are strong, compensation cannot distinguish productive investment from biased expansion; therefore, a spending cap alone is optimal.

items.title: A Balanced Parametrization of Correlation Matrices
items.summary: We introduce the balanced correlation parametrization (BCP), which maps positive-definite correlation matrices one-to-one onto the set of symmetric hollow matrices. A key feature of the parametrization is that both the transformation and its inverse are available in closed form. It combines marginal and partial correlations, is inverse-consistent and equivariant under variable permutations and sign changes, and preserves block structure. A novel property of BCP is that it preserves correlation sparsity as the dimension tends to infinity under suitable factor conditions, providing a basis for sparse high-dimensional correlation modeling. An empirical illustration using standardized idiosyncratic daily stock returns for 1,765 equities over 15 years shows that BCP retains the approximate sparsity pattern and magnitudes of shock correlations, and that it yields accurate positive-definite reconstructions under sparse coordinate restrictions.

items.title: Representation Multiplicity in Causal Forests
items.summary: Including covariates alongside strictly monotone transformations can change a causal forest's treatment decisions without adding information. Random feature selection favors covariates represented by these multiple columns. Under stated conditions, I show that this imbalance can persist as samples grow. Treatment effect components associated with other covariates are omitted, attenuated, or recovered depending on their inclusion probabilities and tree depth. Simulations and a job-training replication illustrate sensitivity to redundant transformations. Sampling groups of variables that generate identical splits restores prediction invariance on the grouping data when fitting and randomization are held fixed.

items.title: Contracting for Decision-Relevant Beliefs
items.summary: An expert may misreport her forecast to influence a decision she cares about. We study contracts that elicit both her belief about a verifiable state and her stake in a binary action. If every belief is possible at two distinct stakes, exact incentive compatibility prevents a belief-only mechanism from letting the action depend on the report. Asking about both belief and stake allows the action to respond, but may require implementation rent. For threshold rules, we show that minimum rent equals the cutoff's positive curvature weighted by the belief distribution. The principal therefore chooses a cutoff by balancing virtual surplus against the implementation rent of truthful reporting. We characterize the best cutoff rule and give sufficient conditions under which it is optimal even among randomized mechanisms.

items.title: Designing Persuasive Experiments
items.summary: Incentives in experimental design are often misaligned: experimenters design and finance experiments to seek regulatory approval, while regulators seek to maximize social welfare. This incentive misalignment is especially relevant for Bayesian and adaptive trial designs, which have gained substantial popularity in recent years and have been actively encouraged by the US Food and Drug Administration. We propose a framework to resolve this conflict, wherein regulators set a minimum welfare threshold, and experimenters optimize designs subject to this constraint. It requires no knowledge of experimenters' private preferences or costs and mitigates strategic Bayesian persuasion. By varying the welfare threshold, we can map the Pareto frontier between the experimenter's and regulator's welfare. Under normal priors, Neyman allocation is always the optimal sampling strategy, regardless of specific objectives. We also characterize the optimal stopping rule. A numerical study calibrated to clinical trial data shows sample size reductions of over 48% relative to classical designs attaining the same social welfare.

items.title: Optimal Dynamic Majority-Quorum Rules: Theory and Evidence
items.summary: We study the optimal sequential aggregation of randomly arriving votes from a finite population to identify an unknown majority preference before a fixed deadline, trading off decision accuracy against the cost of delay. The optimal policy is a dynamic majority-quorum rule: a joint, time-varying threshold on vote lead and count, in which quorum and supermajority requirements emerge as the solution to an inference problem about non-participants' preferences. At each date, the continuation region is lens-shaped: the lead required to stop grows with turnout until too few voters remain to overturn it, and it vanishes at the deadline. We characterize conditions under which the boundary is monotone in the stakes, the arrival process, and time. Because the exact boundary admits no closed form, we derive a large-population approximation that reduces the two-dimensional rule onto a single sufficient statistic, and express the rule as a sequential significance test set by a single error tolerance. Calibrated on Polkadot governance data, an out-of-sample evaluation finds that our rule with a 2\% error tolerance halves decision times relative to the incumbent mechanism.

items.title: Conditional Disclosure as a Coordination Device
items.summary: People with controversial views may stay silent rather than speak out alone, though in a large enough group they could speak safely together. A Social Assurance Contract makes disclosure conditional: signed commitments of support stay private until enough people have signed for it to be safe to publish. In contrast, a survey can measure hidden support but does not make identification conditional on enough others joining. I derive the contract's exact advantage over speaking openly, and when that advantage disappears. Such contracts can turn a few people who would speak alone into a larger coalition.

items.title: Pregnancy and Interrupted Schooling: Evidence from Monthly Histories
items.summary: Pregnancy can disrupt schooling before infant care begins. We use monthly histories from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 to study school interruptions during pregnancy and after childbirth and whether students later return to school or earn a diploma or GED. We jointly model conception and sustained interruptions in enrollment, allowing persistent unobserved differences to affect both processes. Under the timing-of-events identifying assumptions, pregnancy raises the monthly interruption rate to nearly four times the rate without pregnancy. Interruption rates are elevated before delivery and remain elevated afterward. After an interruption, students already exposed to pregnancy return to school and earn a diploma or GED less often within two years. These findings show that schooling disruption is already present during pregnancy, before the additional demands of infant care begin.

items.title: Safety Research and the Allocation of Frontier Compute
items.summary: Who should give up compute for AI safety research: customers or capability research? Safety paid for by customers delays no capability. Safety paid for by research slows the frontier, which gives knowledge more time to accumulate but postpones what a finished frontier provides. In a frontier-takeoff model, the cheaper source at a given allocation is set by a threshold in demand capacity. Demand capacity is the share of compute customers can use once the frontier is finished. Research should pay too only when demand capacity lies below the threshold. Where the threshold sits depends on how fast the value of customer services diminishes. In the calibration it rises with the service budget, because each further unit taken from customers costs them more. Safety paid for by customers should come early: its ratio to customer compute falls over the takeoff unless safety productivity rises fast. In a calibration with a tight service budget, early customer-funded safety lowers the probability of catastrophe from 75 to 51 percent. That is within one point of the best rule found that may also slow research.

items.title: Designing Markets for Screening: Optimal Composition and the Geometry of Surplus
items.summary: We characterize the structure of market compositions that generate Pareto efficient outcomes and the geometry of the surplus set in a screening model with type-dependent costs. Maximizing principal or total surplus concentrates the market at the highest type, with all surplus extracted. Agent-oriented optima instead use, rather than suppress, screening: all agents in the market are served, there is no bunching, and a positive share of agents have the highest type and are served efficiently. Separation is valuable even under agent surplus maximization because it propagates information rents. Under a mild cost-curvature condition, each Pareto efficient outcome is implemented by a unique market. Under a stronger cost-curvature condition, the surplus set is convex whenever values are private, or types with no gains from trade can be included in the market. We characterize all surplus outcomes in these cases. Without such types and with type-dependent costs, the surplus set can be nonconvex. Market segmentation generates the missing outcomes but does not increase the maximum agent surplus at any level of principal surplus. We also derive comparative statics along the Pareto frontier and with respect to value-cost co-movement, distinguishing changes in market composition from changes in individual allocations and rents.

items.title: Shaping the Menu: Information Design under Screening
items.summary: How should consumers learn when a seller chooses a menu of product qualities and prices? We study information design when the seller observes the learning policy, but not consumers' private signals, before choosing its menu. Under cost-curvature conditions, we characterize optimal learning when consumer surplus receives greater weight than profit. Even with two valuations, every optimal posterior distribution combines an interval of posterior types with an efficiently served atom at the highest valuation. The induced menu features a continuum of differentiated products. Strikingly, optimal learning can also induce a lower posterior atom, separated from this interval by a support gap. Buyers in this atom either purchase an isolated low-quality product or are excluded, even when trade with every buyer creates gains. Both configurations can be optimal for the same prior and welfare weight. Served buyers with distinct posterior types are never bunched at the same quality. General finite priors can yield several separating regions and trading atoms. We also characterize the optimal joint design of learning and valuation-dependent segmentation, showing, among other results, that every posterior type with positive gains from trade must be served. Joint design can raise both consumer surplus and profit relative to buyer-optimal private learning alone. Even random assignment to segments with different learning policies and separate menus can give consumers more surplus than any single market yielding the same profit. Additional price discrimination can therefore benefit consumers, even when privacy restrictions require segmentation to reveal nothing about valuations to the seller.

items.title: Truthful Production Uncertainty in Electricity Markets: A Two-Stage Mechanism
items.summary: Renewable power sources have low production costs, but may result in high balancing costs due to the inherent production uncertainty. Current day-ahead markets elicit only point production profiles and neglect the degree of uncertainty associated with each generating asset, preventing the market operator from accounting for balancing costs in day-ahead dispatch and ancillary service procurement. This increases the total system cost and undermines market efficiency, especially in renewable-heavy power systems. To address this, we propose a new market clearing paradigm based on a two-stage mechanism, where producers report their production forecast distribution in the day-ahead stage, followed by the realized production in the real-time stage. By extending the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) payments to the two-stage setting, we show appealing properties in terms of incentive compatibility and individual rationality. An electricity market case study validates the theoretical claims, illustrating the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism in reducing system cost.

items.title: The Robustness of Sequential Implementation under Information Perturbations
items.summary: Bayesian monotonicity is a necessary condition for full implementation in Bayes-Nash equilibrium. Under the sequential equilibrium refinement, however, multi-stage mechanisms can expand the scope for implementation. We show that this additional implementation power is fragile. Whenever a multi-stage mechanism sequentially implements a social choice correspondence that is not Bayesian monotone, we construct arbitrarily small "information perturbations" and show that there are sequential equilibria under these perturbations that yield inadmissible decisions with probability bounded away from zero. Under these perturbations, players' types are not independent conditional on the state and some player is sometimes uncertain of their payoff type. We show by example that the general result fails if perturbations are required to satisfy conditional independence or "known payoff types."

items.title: Higher-Order Neyman Orthogonality in Moment-Condition Models
items.summary: We construct moment functions that are Neyman-orthogonal to a chosen order in parametric moment condition models involving nuisance parameters. These moment functions reduce sensitivity to estimation error in the nuisance parameters and, as such, offer a unified and tractable route to higher-order debiasing in a wide range of econometric models. The number of additional nuisance parameters required by our construction, beyond those already present in the original moment conditions, is independent of the order of orthogonalization and can be reduced to a single scalar if desired.

items.title: Renewable Natural Resources, Regime Shift and Hysteresis
items.summary: Many of the world's renewable resources are in decline. Optimal harvests with smooth recruitment is well studied but in recent years, ecologists have concluded that tipping points in recruitment are common. Recruitment with a tipping point has low-fecundity below the tipping point and high-fecundity above. When the discounted value of high-fecundity is sufficiently high, there is a high-fecundity steady-state. This steady-state is stable but in some cases, small perturbations may result in large, temporary reductions in recruitment and harvests. Below the tipping point, a low-fecundity steady-state need not exist. When a low-fecundity steady-state does exist, there is an endogenous tipping (Skiba) point: below, harvests converge to the low-fecundity steady-state and above, an austere harvest policy transitions the renewable resource to high-fecundity recruitment. If there is hysteresis in recruitment, the high steady-state may not be stable. Moreover, if the high-/low-fecundity differential is large then following a downward perturbation, fecundity optimally remains low.

items.title: Who and How? Adverse Selection and flexible Moral Hazard
items.summary: We characterize incentive-compatible mechanisms in environments with hidden types and flexible hidden actions. Our approach introduces extended recommendation schedules that also prescribe actions off path, after misreports. This yields a tractable and complete characterization of incentive compatibility, which includes a generalized integral monotonicity condition capturing the interaction between adverse selection and moral hazard. We illustrate the usefulness of the characterization in a range of applications, including franchise agreements, employment contracts, and optimal taxation, covering both risk neutrality and risk aversion, with and without limited liability. Among other results, we identify a broad class of environments in which menus of affine contracts are optimal for a profit maximizing principal.

items.title: Linear Demand Systems are Consistent with Discrete Choice
items.summary: Aggregate linear demand systems can be micro-founded by a population of heterogeneous consumers making discrete choices. They can also be extended to incorporate income effects. I prove these results and show how to structurally estimate this class of models using only market-level data. The distribution of consumer preferences is recovered by disciplining the corner solutions with aggregate terms only. This approach allows for the same richness of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) [BLP] while retaining the analytical and computational advantages of linear demand: it does not require exogenously fixing market size, allows for heterogeneity in choice sets, and results in a flexible substitution matrix which varies endogenously as different consumers enter/exit the market. The discrete-choice microfoundation facilitates welfare analysis and the flexible measurement of markups an cost pass-throughs, among a wide range of other applications.

items.title: Smart Lotteries in School Choice: Ex-ante Pareto-Improvement with Ex-post Stability
items.summary: In school choice, students typically have strict preferences over the schools while the schools have coarse priorities over the students based on their distance and their enrolled siblings. The outcome of a centralized admission mechanism is then usually obtained by the Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm with random tie-breaking. Therefore, every outcome of this mechanism that occurs with a positive probability is a stable solution for the coarse priorities. This implies a probabilistic assignment, specifying the admission probability for each student-school pair. In this paper, we propose a new efficiency-improving stable 'smart lottery' mechanism. We aim to improve the probabilistic assignment ex-ante in a stochastic dominance sense, while ensuring that the improved random matching is still ex-post stable, meaning that it can be decomposed into stable matchings regarding the original coarse priorities. Therefore, this smart lottery mechanism can provide a clear Pareto-improvement in expectation for any cardinal utilities compared to the standard DA with lottery solution, without sacrificing the stability of the final outcome. We show that although the underlying computational problem is NP-hard, we can solve the problem in practice by using column generation. Our computational results show that the welfare gains by our mechanism are substantially larger than the expected gains by standard methods that realize efficiency improvements after ties have already been broken. Additionally, we illustrate for real-world school choice data of Ghent (Belgium) that, while not theoretically guaranteed, our mechanism can Pareto-improve upon methods that improve upon DA but violate ex-post stability, such as Efficiency-Adjusted Deferred Acceptance.

items.title: Optimal growth under irreversible pollution: The Forster-Ramsey model
items.summary: We study optimal growth in a Ramsey economy with irreversible pollution, where the natural absorption capacity is non-monotonic and non-concave a la Forster. In the absence of pollution control, the capital dynamics decouple from pollution, and we characterize a simple threshold on the maximal absorption capacity above which the optimal path is sustainable and below which an optimal regime of irreversible pollution sets in. We then introduce an optimal abatement pollution control to assess whether irreversible pollution ceases to be optimal. We derive a four-dimensional dynamical system for capital, consumption, pollution and the (shadow) cost of pollution, coupled with an algebraic rule for optimal abatement. First, we show that while optimal abatement does shift the irreversibility threshold, it may not rule out optimal irreversible pollution paths. Second, and more importantly, we show that embedding the Forster's pollution dynamics into a Ramsey growth model generates a novel and robust hybrid ecological-economic irreversibility condition that is invisible in pollution-only frameworks. Coupling ecosystem curvature with the social discount rate, it is structurally robust and preeminent over all feasibility conditions amenable to policy intervention, and defines the boundary between a world where sustainability is achievable and one where it is not.

items.title: Is the business of frontier AI companies selling tokens? Value capture and equity prices
items.summary: We examine business models that could support frontier AI companies' valuations and the public evidence of plans to earn income beyond selling model access. Reverse cash-flow calculations for OpenAI and Anthropic yield combined year-ten revenue requirements of \$2.79 trillion or \$733 billion, depending on financial assumptions. Public documents identify proposed payments and ownership interests that could supply additional income, such as through partnerships on pharmaceuticals, robotics, or materials science. We discuss how these arrangements relate to firm boundaries and value capture.

items.title: Principal Component Analysis for High-Dimensional Approximate Factor Models in Time Series: Assumptions, Asymptotic Theory, and Identification
items.summary: We consider estimation of large approximate factor models in high-dimensional panels of stationary time series using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). We review the key results establishing the necessary and sufficient conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimators, which hold when both the cross-sectional dimension $n$ and the sample size $T$ tend to infinity. Special emphasis is placed on identification. First, we show that the common and idiosyncratic components are identified only in the limit $n\to\infty$. Second, we discuss the restrictions required to uniquely determine factors and loadings and examine their consequences for statistical inference.

items.title: Two-Sided Plausibility Constraints in Persuasion
items.summary: A sender with commitment provides additional information to an already informed receiver. Final posterior means must be more dispersed than initial means and less dispersed than the state, in convex order. We characterize when these two plausibility constraints are also sufficient, so that every distribution satisfying them can be induced. If the state has a positive density, they are sufficient exactly under interval-partition information: the receiver learns which interval of a partition contains the state and nothing more, where an interval may be a single point. Otherwise, a nonempty open set of distributions satisfying both constraints cannot be induced, even when the sender observes the receiver's information. We use the sufficient case to derive an optimal symmetric disclosure rule in a second-price auction where bidders initially know valuation intervals.

items.title: Decomposing Wage Stagnation: Employment Reallocation, Wage Structure,and Demographics
items.summary: Japan's average log real hourly wages rose from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, declined through the mid-2010s, and partially recovered thereafter. This paper decomposes these changes from 1980 to 2024 into four components: demographic change across worker types, employment reallocation across job types, changes in relative wage structure across job types, and unweighted mean wage growth. The first two represent different margins of adjustment in employment, while the latter two represent different margins of adjustment in wages. The framework combines a shift-share decomposition across worker types with an augmented Olley-Pakes decomposition across job types within worker types. Employment reallocation reflects changes in employment shares across job types, whereas changes in relative wage structure reflect changes in average log wages within job types that alter wage differences across job types. The contributions of the four components vary across periods. Before 1996, unweighted mean wage growth and changes in relative wage structure contribute positively, while demographic change and employment reallocation contribute negatively. During the 1996-2014 period, unweighted mean wage growth and changes in relative wage structure turn negative, so that all four components are negative. After 2014, the recovery mainly reflects unweighted mean wage growth. The contributions from employment reallocation and changes in relative wage structure differ not only between full-time and part-time jobs but also across establishment sizes and industries within employment type. The paper uses the same framework to decompose changes in Japan's gender wage gap.

items.title: Is Inference Conditional on Not Rejecting a Pre-test Less Reliable than Unconditional Inference?
items.summary: Researchers often report an estimate and confidence interval only if a specification test does not reject - for example, only if a pre-trend test supports a difference-in-differences design. Does this make the reported confidence interval less reliable? We show that when the identifying assumptions hold, the answer is no: conditional on passing the pre-test, the confidence interval may over-cover but cannot under-cover. When the assumptions fail, pre-testing can reduce coverage, but under an additional condition it still improves coverage relative to not pre-testing. A calibration to 12 differences-in-differences examples suggests modest effects of pre-testing on coverage.

items.title: Convex Choice
items.summary: For multidimensional Euclidean type spaces, we study convex choice: from any choice set, the set of types that make the same choice is convex. We establish that, in a suitable sense, this property characterizes the sufficiency of local incentive constraints. Convex choice is also of interest more broadly, e.g., in cheap-talk games. We tie convex choice to a notion of directional single-crossing differences (DSCD). For an expected-utility agent choosing among lotteries, DSCD implies that preferences are either one-dimensional or must take the affine form that has been tractable in multidimensional mechanism design.

items.title: Incentive Contracts and Peer Effects in the Workplace
items.summary: We analyze how firms should design wage contracts when workers collaborate in teams and effort costs depend on colleagues through a peer network. Performance-based compensation generates incentives that cascade through the organization, which firms target to boost profits. We analyze optimal incentive design if firms can---and can't---fully discriminate across workers, and when the production technology is separable or complementary across divisions. When workers' effort is substitutable, the most central workers---those who influence most colleagues directly and indirectly---receive the steepest incentives only when output risk is sufficiently large; otherwise firms prioritize workers who are closer to those they influence. When production technology exhibits complementarity across teams, stronger incentives are assigned to workers who influence colleagues in small teams that receive little influence from others. For high levels of output risk, we derive a sufficient network statistic that approximates the profit loss when firms must compensate workers of varying centrality equally. Finally, we apply our findings to organizational design questions, such as optimal firm structure and workforce investments.

items.title: Intentionally Overidentifying Local Projections
items.summary: Local projections (LPs) have become a standard tool for estimating dynamic effects in macroeconomics and are typically implemented using ordinary least squares (OLS) for a given lag order. We propose an alternative approach that exploits additional lags as excluded instrumental variables (IVs). Under a finite-order model with martingale-difference shocks, the resulting (optimally weighted) IV estimator is never asymptotically less efficient than OLS and, as we show, can deliver substantial efficiency gains when data are persistent. For the unit-root AR(1) data with i.i.d. errors, our baseline IV estimator (with one overidentifying restriction) has asymptotic variance $2-h^{-1}$, compared with $h$, the asymptotic variance of the OLS lag-augmented estimator in Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021), for an integer propagation horizon $h$. We then develop IV-based LP inference that is robust to unknown persistence and moderate local model misspecification, whereas the recursive VAR-based inference is generally not robust to the latter. We also characterize the trade-off between the degree of misspecification and the number of additional lag controls. Through simulations and an empirical application, we demonstrate that the proposed method can yield meaningfully shorter confidence intervals for impulse responses than OLS in finite samples.

items.title: When Do Markets Work? Multiplex Networks and Efficiency
items.summary: We study an Arrow-Debreu economy with externalities generated by multiplex networks. Market equilibrium prices reflect not only preferences and the scarcity of goods, but also consumers' network positions induced by goods-specific externalities and the linkages across goods arising from the endogenous budget constraint. We quantify the departures of equilibrium allocations from Pareto efficiency using both a utility-based measure of efficiency loss and a coefficient of resource utilization, thereby linking network multiplexity quantitatively to equilibrium performance. These measures also identify zero-efficiency-loss cases: competitive equilibria are efficient when the relevant network-centrality vectors are parallel, a condition satisfied, in particular, when all networks are regular or when all layers share the same network structure. When competitive markets allocate goods inefficiently, a Lindahl equilibrium implemented through personalized prices can restore efficiency, although it may leave some consumers worse off.

items.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
items.summary: We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020] Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.

items.title: The Gendered Impacts of Perceived Skin Tone: Evidence from African American Siblings in 1870-1940
items.summary: We study differences in economic outcomes by perceived skin tone among African Americans using full-count U.S. decennial census data from the late-19th and early-20th centuries. Comparing children coded as "Black" or "Mulatto" by census enumerators and linking these children across population censuses, we first document large gaps in educational attainment and income among African Americans with darker and lighter perceived skin tones. To disentangle the drivers of these gaps, we identify all 35,992 families in which enumerators assigned same-gender siblings different Black/Mulatto classifications. Relative to sisters coded as Mulatto, sisters coded as Black had lower educational attainment, were less likely to marry, and had less-educated, likely lower-earning husbands. These patterns are consistent with more severe contemporaneous discrimination against African American women with darker perceived skin tones. In contrast, we find similar educational attainment, marital outcomes, and incomes among differently-classified brothers. Men perceived as African Americans of any skin tone faced similar contemporaneous discrimination, consistent with the "one-drop" racial classification rule that grouped together individuals with any known Black ancestry. Lower incomes for African American men perceived as having darker skin tone in the general population were driven by differences in opportunities and resources that varied across families, likely reflecting the impacts of historical or family-level discrimination.

items.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
items.summary: Estimating the first stage of an instrumental variables (IV) model with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary of technical instruments and a penalty level. First-order asymptotic theory offers no guidance on these choices, as any consistent implementation yields a structural parameter estimator with the same limiting distribution. In finite samples, however, these choices can have a substantial impact on the resulting structural parameter estimate. Working in a model with a single endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors, we use first- and second-order Stein identities to derive the approximate mean squared error (AMSE) of the instrumental-variables LASSO (IV-LASSO) estimator, which can be consistently estimated and used to rank a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty candidates. The AMSE reveals a bias-variance trade-off: more complex first-stage fits better approximate the conditional mean of the endogenous variable but are also more correlated with the structural errors, with complexity measured by the degrees of freedom of the LASSO fit. The weight on this bias rises with the endogeneity of the regressor, a quantity that neither plug-in nor cross-validation penalty rules take into account. Despite the AMSE being derived in a Gaussian model, penalty selection by minimizing the feasible AMSE criterion delivers up to a one-third lower mean squared error compared to cross-validation and plug-in penalty rules in Gaussian and non-Gaussian simulation designs calibrated to the data of Gilchrist and Sands (2016).

items.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
items.summary: AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model. Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%. Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

items.title: An efficient stochastic generalized method of moments estimator for nonlinear moment models
items.summary: We study the asymptotic properties of the nonlinear stochastic GMM algorithm proposed by Chen, Lee, Liao, Seo, Shin and Song for recursively estimating parameters defined by possibly nonlinear and overidentified moment restrictions $\E[g(X,β^*)]=0$. Each observation updates estimates of the moment Jacobian, inverse covariance matrix and Gauss--Newton preconditioner at a cost independent of sample size. For linear and nonlinear instrumental-variable moments, we derive an exact rank-two Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury update. The algorithm combines preconditioned stochastic approximation with iterate averaging. Under a preconditioned monotonicity condition, satisfied globally in linear models and locally around a consistent pilot estimate in general, we establish almost sure convergence and rates, as well as a functional central limit theorem with the efficient GMM variance. These results require four moments of the moment function and its Jacobian when the step exponent exceeds $2/3$. The inverse Gauss--Newton matrix consistently estimates this variance, and a projected linearised statistic enables online testing of overidentifying restrictions. We extend the results to $L$-dependent data with long-run variance weights under stronger moment assumptions. Simulations show that the averaged estimator approaches offline two-step GMM in accuracy and coverage at $10^6$ observations, while requiring a fraction of its computing time and fixed memory at up to $10^7$ observations. The online test achieves correct size and comparable power. In an application estimating the effect of a third child on weeks worked using $254{,}654$ women from the 1980 US Census, single-pass estimates agree with offline GMM within a fraction of a standard error on average across data orderings, and both methods yield the same overidentification-test conclusion in most orderings.

items.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
items.summary: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.

items.title: Identification, Estimation and Inference Based on Constructed Instruments
items.summary: We propose a structural projection (SP) method for identifying and estimating structural parameters in regression models associated with endogenous regressors. The method projects the structural error onto the sigma-field generated by the regressors, decomposing it into a conditional mean component and an orthogonal residual. This decomposition yields an internally constructed instrument that is valid whenever the conditional mean lies in a known subspace, avoiding the need for external instruments. We establish identification conditions, derive consistency and asymptotic normality for the resulting estimator, and propose a LASSO-based selection procedure for choosing the subspace when no natural candidate is available. The SP method applies to a broad class of linear, nonlinear, and non-separable models. Simulations show that SP substantially outperforms least-squares-based benchmarks under endogeneity while remaining competitive when it is absent, and we illustrate the method using data on the returns to schooling.

items.title: Endogenous Information Design and Informational Evolution in Dynamic Economic Systems with Incentives and Learning
items.summary: This paper studies the endogenous informational evolution of dynamic economic systems. Building on Hurwicz's conceptual framework, such a system is defined as a dynamic joint adjustment process of resource and information allocation linked by recursive feedback. Economic theory gains precision by isolating particular margins, but when information production, disclosure, learning, incentives, actions, and future feasibility interact across these two processes, conclusions obtained by holding other margins fixed need not survive their joint determination. The paper develops a system-level dynamic equilibrium framework for this interaction. Holding particular links fixed yields familiar environments in dynamic mechanism design, information design, experimentation and learning, feedback and disclosure, and information acquisition. The analysis establishes three central failures relative to fixed or partially exogenous informational environments: informational efficiency under exogenous feasibility is generally incompatible with endogenous dynamic feasibility; incentive and disclosure design cannot generally be separated; and informational monotonicity can fail without implementation replicability. It also identifies the corresponding positive boundaries. Optimal disclosure may be interior or extreme; bang--bang disclosure arises under additional conditions, and a further specialization generates an endogenous transition from opacity to transparency. Information may therefore be optimally withheld even when its direct decision value is strictly positive. Extensions to private payoff-relevant information and limited commitment preserve the recursive structure.

items.title: GMM for Panel Data Quantile Regression
items.summary: This paper develops a smoothed generalized method of moments (GMM) framework for panel quantile models with individual-specific fixed-effects and endogenous regressors. By smoothing the indicator in the quantile moment conditions and profiling out the individual effects through smoothed individual quantile restrictions, the proposed estimator can be implemented using standard GMM algorithms. We establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and feasible inference under weak time dependence as both panel dimensions diverge. This dependence structure accommodates dynamic panel specifications, serially dependent disturbances, lagged instruments, and within-individual heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent inference. Monte Carlo simulations show that the estimator is nearly unbiased under endogeneity and yields generally accurate inference while remaining computationally tractable. An application to OECD inflation dynamics suggests asymmetric inflation propagation: under the structural IVQR interpretation, the response of current inflation to lagged inflation is substantially larger at the lower structural quantile than at the upper structural quantile.

items.title: Predicting the Distribution of Treatment Effects: A Covariate-Adjustment Approach
items.summary: Important questions for impact evaluation require knowledge not only of average effects, but of the distribution of treatment effects. The inability to observe individual counterfactuals makes answering these empirical questions challenging. I propose an inference approach for points of the distribution of treatment effects that uses predicted counterfactuals through covariate adjustment. I provide finite-sample valid inference using sample-splitting and asymptotically valid inference using cross-fitting under arguably weak conditions. Revisiting five randomized controlled trials on microcredit that reported null average effects, I find important distributional impacts, with some individuals helped and others harmed by the increased credit access.

items.title: Two-Sided Market Power in Firm-to-Firm Trade
items.summary: We develop and estimate a model of two-sided market power to study tariff pass-through in firm-to-firm trade. A tariff moves the negotiated price through two channels: the bilateral markup, set by bargaining, and the supplier's marginal cost, which falls alongside quantities under decreasing returns. The same decreasing returns give concentrated buyers rents to bargain over, so prices fall with the buyer's share of its supplier's output. Using U.S. customs data, we estimate substantial importer bargaining power and steep export supply. Within continuing relationships, suppliers absorb about 30 percent of the 2018 tariffs, primarily through lower marginal costs as demand contracts.

items.title: Childcare Waitlists
items.summary: Parents seeking childcare often face long waitlists. At the same time, vacancies at childcare centers can remain unfilled for extended periods. We trace this paradox to two persistent features of childcare services. First, families consider multiple child care options due to enrollment uncertainties, resulting in phantom listings that remain on waitlists even after families have found care elsewhere or no longer need a slot. Second, filling a slot is time-consuming: centers learn whether a family is actively seeking enrollment only after making an offer and waiting for a response. As families pursue alternatives while they wait and their children age, these delays and feedback effects amplify the mismatch between demand and available capacity. We study two operational remedies. First, we examine regular verification that removes phantom listings before offers are made, improving the efficiency of enrollment and reducing vacancies. Second, we study mixed-age classrooms, in which some slots designated for older children can be flexibly used by younger children. This flexibility increases utilization, shortens waits, and reduces wasted offers. Its benefits extend beyond conventional pooling: as children move between age groups, classrooms can be filled through internal flows rather than costly external search, further reducing enrollment delays. Together, verification and mixed use offer a way to expand effective capacity in early childhood classrooms, where regulatory and operational constraints make adding physical capacity particularly costly.

items.title: Complementarity, Augmentation, or Substitutivity? The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on the U.S. Federal Workforce
items.summary: This study applies a multi-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation system, which grounds large language model assessments in curated evidence, to evaluate generative AI's near-term impact on knowledge, skills, and abilities across several hundred federal occupational series. Each occupation is scored along three dimensions of complementarity (AI enhances existing competencies), augmentation (AI requires workers to transform competencies), and substitutivity (AI replaces human tasks). Results reveal that generative AI primarily complements and augments federal roles, with limited substitution potential. Even occupations scoring highest on substitutivity reflect partial automation of routine subtasks rather than position elimination. These findings caution against blunt workforce reductions premised on displacement and instead support targeted reskilling, competency-based planning, and human-AI collaboration. The framework is adaptable to other organizations with structured competency models and job documentation.

items.title: Simple Standard Errors for Complicated (Quasi-)Experimental Designs
items.summary: We develop standard errors for estimates of causal effects in settings where the distribution of treatment exposures is known but potentially exhibits complicated dependence patterns across units. Such dependence arises, for example, in settings with spillovers/interference across units or when the treatment assignment is spatially correlated. Our variance estimator generalizes several properties of the Neyman variance estimator for completely randomized experiments to general designs: it is unbiased for an upper bound on the variance from the design-based perspective; the conservativeness of this upper bound depends on the heterogeneity of treatment effects; and it is also valid under certain forms of super-population sampling of the potential outcomes. Our estimator reduces to standard approaches in simple designs, such as the Neyman variance estimator in completely randomized experiments and the cluster-robust variance estimator in cluster-randomized experiments. We show that the proposed estimator is admissible among the class of quadratic-form variance estimators, and derive asymptotic conditions under which it is consistent for an upper bound on the asymptotic variance of the treatment effect estimator. In simulations and applications based on two empirical studies, one with peer effects and another with a spatially correlated treatment, we find that the proposed variance estimator performs well, and in some cases yields standard errors that are 2-3 times shorter than those of existing alternatives.

items.title: Policy design in experiments with unknown interference
items.summary: This paper studies experimental designs for estimation and inference on policies with spillover effects. Units are organized into a finite number of large clusters and interact in unknown ways within each cluster. First, we introduce a single-wave experiment that estimates the marginal effect of a change in treatment probabilities, taking spillover effects into account. Using the marginal effect, we propose a policy optimality test and improve the population's average outcome through marginal changes. Second, we design a multi-wave experiment to estimate optimal treatment rules, with strong regret guarantees. We provide an implementation in a large-scale field experiment studying climate adaptation.

items.title: Economic Impacts of Climate Change in the United States: Integrating and Harmonizing Evidence from Recent Studies
items.summary: This paper synthesizes evidence on climate change impacts specific to U.S. populations. We develop an apples-to-apples comparison of econometric studies that empirically estimate the relationship between climate change and gross domestic product (GDP). We demonstrate that with harmonized probabilistic socioeconomic and climate inputs these papers project a narrower and lower range of 2100 GDP losses than what is reported across the published studies, yet the implied U.S.-specific social cost of greenhouse gases (SC-GHG) is still greater than the market-based damage estimates in current enumerative models. We also take a first step in integrating evidence on nonmarket damages with the GDP impacts. Our findings highlight the need for more research addressing the limitations of macroeconomic empirical studies and research on nonmarket and international spillover impacts. Further investigation of how macroeconomic and enumerative approaches can be integrated would enhance the usefulness of both strands of literature to climate policy analysis going forward.

items.title: Endogenous shareholding auctions
items.summary: We introduce endogenous shareholding auctions for production economies where a designer must elicit demand in order to determine price and quantity. Each of these auctions has the property that the auction's profit is distributed across the designer and the bidders in accordance with ownership shares that are determined over the course of the auction. We characterize this class, and a larger class, on the basis of standard axioms. Finally, we investigate optimal auctions according to both prior-free domination and subjective expected welfare. Applications include public housing, voluntary separation, and monopoly regulation.
